HOW TO USE THIS BOOK

12 mock testsListening + Reading

This book contains twelve complete Multilevel mock tests in the real exam format. Treat each one like the real exam: keep to the time, write on the answer sheet and check your score.

🎧
Listening

6 parts · 35 questions. Scan the QR / open the channel and play the audio for each test. Each recording is played twice.

📖
Reading

5 parts · 35 questions · 60 minutes. Do the test in one sitting, without a dictionary.

📝
Answer sheets

After each test there is a Multilevel answer sheet — write your answers there, just like the real exam.

🔑
Answer key & scripts

Check your answers and count your score out of 35. Then read the listening scripts at the back to see what you missed.

📈
Track progress

Repeat the mocks after a few weeks and compare your scores.

How modern smartphones work

I. Modern smartphones are designed to be sleek, lightweight, and durable. Most use materials like aluminum, glass, or plastic to create a stylish yet strong outer shell. The design isn’t just about looks—it also protects the internal components from damage. Some phones are even water-resistant, allowing users to take calls in the rain or accidentally drop their device in water without serious harm. Manufacturers carefully choose materials that balance weight, strength, and cost, while also considering how the phone feels in the hand.

II. At the heart of every smartphone is a powerful processor, often referred to as the “chip.” This tiny but complex piece of hardware controls everything—from opening apps and browsing the internet to playing videos and managing memory. The processor works with other components like RAM and storage to ensure smooth performance. Faster processors allow users to multitask easily and enjoy high-quality games or videos without delays. In short, the processor is the brain that keeps the smartphone running efficiently.

III. Smartphones allow people to stay connected wherever they go. Thanks to mobile networks, users can make calls, send texts, and use mobile data to access the internet. Wi-Fi connections offer even faster speeds at home, work, or public places. Bluetooth lets users connect wirelessly to headphones, speakers, and other devices. GPS helps with navigation, showing real-time directions and location tracking. These features make smartphones essential tools for communication, travel, and daily life

I

V. The touchscreen is one of the most important parts of a smartphone. It allows users to interact with the device using simple gestures like tapping, swiping, or pinching. Beneath the glass surface is a layer that senses touch and sends signals to the processor. This technology makes smartphones easy to use and highly responsive. Whether typing a message, playing a game, or zooming in on a photo, the touchscreen provides a smooth and intuitive experience. V. Smartphone cameras have improved dramatically in recent years. Many devices now include multiple lenses for wide-angle shots, close-ups, and even night photography. The camera uses sensors to capture light and convert it into digital images. Advanced software helps enhance photos by adjusting brightness, contrast, and focus. Users can also record high-definition videos and edit them directly on their phones. For many people, their smartphone has replaced traditional cameras entirely.

VI. Security is a major concern for smartphone users. These devices store sensitive information like passwords, contacts, photos, and banking details. To protect this data, smartphones use features like fingerprint scanners, facial recognition, and PIN codes. Encryption helps keep messages and files safe from hackers. Regular software updates also fix security issues and improve protection. With so much personal data on our phones, strong security features are more important than ever.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for question 21-29.

THE ICE AGE

The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old and there have actually been about 11 different Ice Ages. An Ice Age is a cold period in which glaciers, slowly moving sheets or masses of ice, covered much of the Earth's surface. The last ice age on Earth was called 'The Great Ice Age' occurring about 11,000 years ago. Over 1/3 of the Earth's surface was covered in ice, and the air had less carbon dioxide in it.

Two explanations are usually given as to why the ice ages occurred. One, the temperatures were so cold that it never rained, only snowed. Two, the tilt of the Earth changed and it was away from the Sun.

The land looks much different during an ice age. It is frozen and bare land which is called a tundra. Very few plants exist on a tundra since the ground is too frozen to sustain life. There are evergreen trees that grow but there is no grass or flowers, only shrubs, bushes, and moss grass. In some parts of the world there are still tundra in parts of North America, Europe, and Asia.

Following the end of the last Ice Age there were glaciers left behind and the sheets of ice-covered rivers and valleys. The melting and the refreezing of the ice continued to occur for millions of years. Then, about 10,000 years ago the Earth began to get warmer and the remaining glaciers melted leaving lakes and valleys with a mixture of rocks and soil. However, in the higher elevations there was still ice and glaciers, including some today that were left over from the last Ice Age.

A scientist named Louis Aggasiz studied the clues of the ice age in the 1800s. He explained to other scientists that boulders they saw were left by glaciers and carrying them many miles from one area to another. The other scientists did not believe him. However, Aggasiz proved his theory because boulders the glaciers left behind were made of granite. There were no other granite boulders in the area so they had to have been brought there by the glaciers. Other things also proved his theory. There was polished bedrock, large sand and gravel piles, big valleys, and rough mountain tops, which were all formed by the movement of the glaciers during the ice age. Even though ice ages took place, there were still animals living on the Earth including the wooly mammoth, wooly rhinos, cave bears, horses, wolves, bison and reindeer. A few of them are now extinct such as the woolly mammoth, cave bear, and woolly rhino. Scientists know they existed though because there were people who painted pictures of the animals on the sides of the caves where they lived.

There have been skeletons of the animals found as well. In addition, cuts of bones have been found in these skeletons which were made by the knives of the hunters. Some of the knives the hunters used were found next to the skeletons too. People also lived during the Ice Age 35,000 years ago. The role of the men included hunting for food, and the women and children prepared the food, made clothing from the hides of animals, and built the shelters where everyone lived. When the hunters killed an animal, every part of the animal was useful. Its meat and organs were used for food. The skins were used for their clothing, blankets, and shelter. Even an animal's stomach was used for carrying water. Finally, the bones were used for needles, weapons, and different tools.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

HOW VACCINES WORK

For more than two hundred years, vaccines have been one of the most powerful tools in modern medicine. They have helped people live longer, healthier lives by preventing diseases that once killed millions. To understand how vaccines work, it is useful to first look at how the human immune system protects the body, what happens when a vaccine is given, and why vaccines are so important for both individuals and communities.

The human body has a defense system called the immune system. Its main job is to protect us from harmful invaders, such as viruses and bacteria. When these invaders, also known as pathogens, enter the body, the immune system recognizes them as dangerous and starts fighting. One of the most important parts of the immune system is the white blood cells. These cells move through the bloodstream and tissues, always searching for signs of infection. When they detect a virus or bacterium, some white blood cells attack and destroy the invaders directly, while others create special proteins called antibodies. Antibodies are like tiny weapons that attach to the virus or bacterium, making it easier for the body to remove it.

An important feature of the immune system is memory. After fighting an infection once, the immune system “remembers” the invader. If the same pathogen enters the body again, the immune system responds faster and more effectively, often stopping the disease before it can make a person sick. This natural memory is what vaccines use to give us protection.

A vaccine is a medical product that trains the immune system without causing the actual disease. It works by showing the body a safe version of a pathogen. This can be done in several ways. Some vaccines use pathogens that are killed so they cannot cause disease. Others use a version of the virus or bacterium that is alive but weakened. Some vaccines include only parts of the pathogen, such as proteins on its surface. In recent years, new vaccines have been made with mRNA, which gives the body instructions to make a harmless piece of the pathogen’s protein so the immune system can learn to recognize it.

When a person receives a vaccine, usually by injection, their immune system reacts as if it were facing a real infection. White blood cells create antibodies and memory cells. However, because the vaccine is not dangerous, the person does not experience the severe symptoms of the actual disease. Later, if the real pathogen tries to attack, the immune system is ready to fight it quickly.

Before vaccines existed, infectious diseases caused enormous suffering. Smallpox, for example, killed millions of people for centuries. In the 20th century alone, smallpox caused more than 300 million deaths. Thanks to vaccines, smallpox was completely eliminated in 1980, the first disease in history to be wiped out by human effort. Other diseases, such as polio, measles, and diphtheria, have also been greatly reduced by vaccination campaigns. In many countries today, children rarely see these illnesses, which were once common and deadly.

Vaccines not only protect individuals but also communities. This is because of a concept called herd immunity. When enough people are vaccinated, the disease has little chance to spread. This protects those who cannot receive vaccines, such as newborn babies or people with certain medical conditions.

Some people worry about the safety of vaccines. Like any medicine, vaccines can have side effects. These are usually mild, such as a sore arm or a slight fever. Serious side effects are extremely rare. Scientists and doctors carefully test vaccines before they are approved, and they continue to monitor them to make sure they remain safe. Another question people often ask is why we sometimes need booster shots. The reason is that immune memory can fade over time. For some diseases, like measles, one or two doses are enough to provide lifelong protection. For others, like tetanus or COVID-19, booster doses may be needed to keep the immune system strong.

Vaccines are not only for children. Adults also benefit from them. For example, older people often receive vaccines against influenza or pneumonia, because their immune systems are weaker. Travelers may need vaccines before visiting certain countries where diseases such as yellow fever are present. In recent years, new technologies have made it possible to develop vaccines more quickly. The COVID-19 pandemic showed how important this can be. Scientists created safe and effective vaccines in less than a year, something that would have seemed impossible in the past. These vaccines helped reduce severe illness and death worldwide. At the same time, the pandemic also showed the challenges of vaccine distribution. In some places, vaccines were not available for everyone at the same time. This highlighted the need for global cooperation, since diseases can easily cross borders.

His second name came from the Law Department that Vaska enjoyed visiting.

Having lost interest in law, the cat settled at the front entrance to the Hermitage. There he played a more important role as a porter and got more food. Every morning half an hour before opening, he called the guards to the doors with a loud mew. When the first visitors entered the hall, he would lay by the stairs to get more attention.

Among the visitors there were many volunteers to help take care of the cats. Today the museum covers the cats' living expenses. Also, there are Sponsors eager to take part. On Cats' Day visitors are allowed into the basement to watch the cats' everyday life. Some cats are available for adoption and people are happy to take them home as a symbol of the Hermitage.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

Now it is becoming clear that group decisions are also extremely valuable for the success of social animals, such as ants, bees. birds and dolphins. Bees make collective decisions, and they do it rather well, according to Christian List of the London School of Economics, who has studied group decision-making in humans and animals. Researchers led by Dr List looked at colonies once the original colony reaches a certain size. The queen goes off with about two-thirds of the worker bees to live in a new home or nest, leaving a daughter queen in the old nest with the remaining workers. Among the bees that depart are some that have searched for and found some new nest sites, and reported back using a characteristic body movement known as a 'waggle dance' to indicate to the other bees the suitable places they have located. The longer the dance, the better the site. After a while, other bees start to visit the sites signalled by their companions to see for themselves and, on their return, also perform more waggle dances. The process eventually leads to a consensus on the best site and the breakaway swarm migrates. The decision is remarkably reliable, with the bees choosing the best site even when there is only small difference between alternative sites.

But exactly how do bees reach such a robust consensus? To find out, Dr List and his colleagues used a computer-generated model of the decision-making process. By experimenting with it they found that, when bees in the model were very good at finding nesting sites but did not share their information, this dramatically slowed down the migration. leaving the swarm homeless and vulnerable. Conversely. bees in the model blindly following the waggle dances of others without first checking. The researchers concluded that the ability of bees to identify successfully and quickly the best site depends on both the bees ‘interdependence in communicating the whereabouts of the bees’ site, and their independence in confirming this information for themselves.

Another situation in which collective decisions are taken occurs when animals are either isolated from crucial sources of information or dominated by other members of the group. José Halloy of the Free University of Brussels in Belgium used robotic cockroaches to subvert the behaviour of living cockroaches and control their decision-making process. In his experiment, the artificial bugs were introduced to the live ones and soon became sufficiently socially integrated that they were perceived by the real cockroaches as equals. By manipulating the robots, which were in the minority, Halloy was able to persuade the living cockroaches to choose an inappropriate shelter- even one which they had rejected before being infiltrated by the robots.

The way insects put into effect collective decisions can be complex and as important as the decisions themselves. At the University of Bristol, in the UK, Nigel Franks and his colleagues studied how a species of ant establishes a new nest. Franks and his associates reported how the insects reduce the problems associated with making a necessarily swift choice. If the ants’ existing nest become suddenly threatened, the insects choose certain ants to act as scouts to find a new nest.

How quickly they accomplish the transfer to a new home depends not only on how soon the best available site is found, but also on how quickly the migration there can be achieved.

Once the suitable new nest is identified, the chosen ants begin to lead others, which have made it to the new site or which may simply be in the vicinity, back to the original threatened nest. In this way, those ants which are familiar with the route can help transport, for example, the queen and young ants to the new site, and simultaneously show the way to those ants which have been left behind to guard the old nest. In this way moving processes are accomplished faster and more efficiently. Thus, the dynamics of collective decision-making are closely related to the efficient implementation of those decisions. How this might apply to choices that humans make is, as yet, unclear. But it does suggest, even for humans, the importance of recruiting dynamic leaders to a cause, because the most important thing about collective decision-making, as shown by these insect experiments, is to get others to follow.

THE ROSETTA STONE

I. In 1799, during Napoleon's campaign in Egypt, a French soldier named Pierre-François Bouchard made an unexpected discovery in the town of Rosetta. He found a large, dark stone slab inscribed with text. Recognizing its potential importance, the slab was secured. It was immediately clear that this was no ordinary artifact, as it appeared to contain the same text written in three different scripts, presenting a linguistic puzzle that had confused scholars for centuries.

II. The true value of the Rosetta Stone lay in its trilingual inscription. The top section was written in Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, the script of monuments and religious texts which no one at the time could read. The middle section was in Demotic, a more common script used in ancient Egypt for everyday purposes. The bottom section was in Ancient Greek, a language that was well understood by scholars. It was this trilingual format that provided the pivotal clue for finally decoding the lost language of the pharaohs.

III. For over two decades, many scholars attempted to decipher the hieroglyphs with limited success. The final breakthrough came from a young French scholar named Jean-François Champollion. He had dedicated his life to the study of ancient Egypt and, in 1822, he announced his success. By building on the work of others and applying his own profound knowledge of Coptic (a language descended from Ancient Egyptian), he was able to unlock the secrets of the hieroglyphic script.

IV. Champollion's method was both systematic and brilliant. He hypothesized that the hieroglyphs enclosed in oval shapes, known as cartouches, represented the names of royal figures. By comparing the Greek names of pharaohs like Ptolemy and Cleopatra with the hieroglyphs in the corresponding cartouches, he was able to assign phonetic values to many of the hieroglyphic symbols. This phonetic approach, rather than treating each symbol as a picture of a word, was the crucial step that allowed the entire system to be understood.

V. The decipherment of the Rosetta Stone was a watershed moment in history. It didn't just allow one text to be read; it opened the door to understanding thousands of other inscriptions and papyri from ancient Egypt. For the first time, historians could read the history, literature, and religious beliefs of the Egyptians in their own words. This single discovery essentially gave birth to the entire field of modern Egyptology and unveiled the complexities of a civilization that had been silent for nearly two millennia.

VI. After the defeat of the French forces in Egypt in 1801, the Rosetta Stone was transferred to British possession under the terms of a treaty. It has been on public display at the British Museum in London since 1802, where it remains the single most visited object. However, its location is a source of ongoing contention, with Egyptian authorities and cultural heritage groups frequently calling for its repatriation to Egypt, arguing it is a vital piece of their national heritage.

DAYDREAMING

In today’s busy society, people often see daydreaming as a waste of time — a sign that someone is lazy or unable to focus. From classrooms to workplaces, being caught staring into space is usually considered a bad habit that needs to be corrected. However, recent research suggests that allowing our minds to wander freely might actually have important benefits for creativity, problem-solving, and emotional well-being.

For many years, psychologists believed that daydreaming prevented people from concentrating on real-world tasks. But a growing number of scientists now argue that the human brain is never completely at rest. Even when we are not focused on anything in particular, a network in our brain known as the default mode network becomes active. This system is responsible for imagination, self-reflection, and connecting different ideas — all of which are essential for innovative thinking.

Dr. Kalina Christoff, a neuroscientist at the University of British Columbia, has studied the brain activity of people while they daydream. Her research shows that moments of mental drifting can help the brain make unexpected connections, leading to sudden insights. She explains that when the mind is allowed to move freely from one thought to another, it can link distant memories or ideas in original ways — a process that structured, focused thinking often prevents.

To explore this idea further, a group of psychologists conducted an experiment in which participants were asked to perform a creative task after either resting quietly or doing a simple, repetitive activity such as sorting colored paperclips. Those who had a chance to let their minds wander during the dull activity produced more imaginative ideas than those who didn’t. According to the researchers, these results indicate that mild mental distraction gives the subconscious mind time to process information in the background.

Moreover, daydreaming might also play a role in emotional balance. When people think about their goals, memories, or relationships during idle moments, they are engaging in a kind of mental rehearsal that can prepare them for future situations. In moderation, this helps individuals reflect on their feelings and build empathy. However, experts inform that too much or negative daydreaming — for instance, repeatedly imagining stressful or unrealistic scenarios — can lead to anxiety or dissatisfaction.

In the modern world, where people are constantly connected to screens and notifications, genuine mental pauses have become rare. Psychologists suggest that taking short breaks without digital distractions can help restore mental energy and reduce stress. So, rather than trying to eliminate daydreaming, perhaps we should embrace it as a natural and valuable function of the mind.

THE TELECOMMUTING PARADIGM

The paradigm of the traditional workplace is undergoing a seismic shift. Telecommuting, once a niche arrangement, has become increasingly prevalent across numerous sectors. Industries from technology to legal philosophy are progressively embracing flexible work models, permitting staff to operate remotely, at least on a hybrid basis. Nevertheless, the once-futuristic prophecy of near-vacant office buildings—populated only by essential maintenance or on-site personnel—remains a distant reality.

The tangible merits for employers are compelling. A distributed workforce mitigates the necessity for vast, costly office real estate. Furthermore, empirical data suggests a significant uptick in output. North American studies, for instance, indicate that remote employees can be 30-40% more prolific. Manager James Horgan posits that this surge is partially attributable to the elimination of the arduous daily commute. ‘Our findings revealed a pattern of reinvestment; the time recuperated from travel was largely channeled back into professional tasks,’ Horgan explains. ‘This new-found autonomy was highly valued, and in a gesture of reciprocity, employees demonstrated their commitment through heightened productivity.’

Beyond productivity, offering remote work serves as a powerful tool for talent acquisition and retention. The societal dividends are equally profound. Telecommuting fosters greater workforce inclusivity, democratizing access to employment for demographics that have historically faced barriers. This includes not only primary caregivers for the elderly or infirm, but also individuals with disabilities and those residing in geographically isolated regions. An ancillary benefit is the potential for enhanced civic engagement, as the temporal flexibility afforded by remote work allows individuals to participate more fully in local community life.

The endurance of the physical office, however, is rooted in more than mere tradition. Many organizations contend that the serendipitous collaboration and rapid innovation that fuel growth are best fostered in a shared environment. The organic process of mentorship, whereby junior staff absorb professional nuances through informal observation—a kind of corporate osmosis—is notoriously difficult to replicate virtually. The office thus remains a crucial crucible for forging company culture and a tangible sense of collective identity, elements that risk dilution within a fully atomized workforce.

However, this model is not without its detriments. A significant portion of the remote workforce grapples with feelings of isolation and the absence of the spontaneous, collegial camaraderie inherent in a physical office. Moreover, the erosion of clear boundaries between professional duties and personal time can make achieving a sustainable work-life equilibrium challenging. Consequently, it is incumbent upon employers to implement proactive support structures, such as regular virtual team-building activities and robust mental wellness programs, to ensure their distributed teams remain cohesive, motivated, and psychologically sound.

THE CONCEPT OF SMART CITIES

I. A "smart city" is an urban area that uses various types of electronic methods and sensors to collect data. Insights gained from that data are used to manage assets, resources, and services efficiently. The ultimate goal is to improve the quality of life for its citizens by making urban operations and services more effective and responsive to their needs.

II. The foundation of any smart city is a robust and integrated network of information and communication technology (ICT). This includes the Internet of Things (IoT), where everyday objects are embedded with sensors and connected to the internet. These sensors can be placed in everything from streetlights and rubbish bins to public transport and water pipes, all feeding real-time information into a central system for analysis.

III. The practical applications of this technology are vast. For instance, smart traffic management systems can analyze live traffic flow to adjust traffic light timings, reducing congestion and pollution. Smart grids can optimize energy distribution, preventing blackouts and promoting the use of renewable energy. Connected rubbish bins can signal when they are full, allowing for more efficient waste collection routes.

IV. While the potential benefits are significant, the development of smart cities raises serious questions about privacy. The constant collection of data on citizens' movements, energy use, and daily habits could be misused. There is a risk of creating a surveillance society where personal information is vulnerable to cyberattacks or used for social control. Establishing strong data protection regulations and transparent policies is therefore essential.

V. Another critical challenge is ensuring that the benefits of a smart city are accessible to all residents. There is a danger of creating a "digital divide," where those who are less comfortable with technology, often the elderly or low-income groups, are left behind. If services like public transport or healthcare access become primarily app-based, it could create new barriers for those without smartphones or digital literacy skills.

VI. Engagement of residents is a crucial element in the development of smart cities. Without the input of residents, urban planners may develop solutions that fail to address the actual needs of the community. Public consultations, participatory design workshops, and open forums can help ensure that smart city initiatives are inclusive and reflect the priorities of all citizens, fostering trust and collaboration between governments and the public.

THE DIGITAL SHIFT

The transition to remote work was, at first, liberating. For the first few months, I relished the flexibility. No more crowded morning commutes, the freedom to structure my day, and the quiet focus I could achieve without the constant interruptions of a busy office. I felt my productivity soar, and the work-life balance I had long chased seemed finally within my grasp. However, this initial honeymoon phase began to fade as a new kind of pressure slowly crept in: the tyranny of the digital leash.

The source of this pressure wasn't a single policy or a demanding boss, but a collective, unspoken set of expectations that our team had developed. The constant 'ping' of instant messages created an obligation to be perpetually connected. Emails sent late at night seemed to demand an immediate response, blurring the lines between work and personal time until they were almost non-existent. The culture had shifted from 'working from home' to 'living at work'.

This came to a head during a critical project with a tight deadline. I needed some vital data from a colleague, Mark, to complete my section. I sent him a message on our team chat, then an email. Hours passed in what I call 'digital silence'. My anxiety escalated as my mind raced with possibilities – was he ignoring the messages? Was he annoyed about something? I imagined the worst, and my frustration grew, stalling my progress entirely. By late afternoon, I was convinced the project was in jeopardy because of his lack of response.

Just as I was about to escalate the issue to our manager, a call came through from Mark. He sounded apologetic and flustered. It turned out his home internet connection had been down all day, and his messages to me, explaining the situation and providing the data from his phone, had been failing to send due to a temporary network glitch on his end. The fault wasn’t with Mark, but with our communication methods and the assumptions they encouraged. It was an epiphany for me; the real issue wasn't a lack of commitment from anyone, but the chaotic, high-anxiety system of communication we had fallen into.

That evening, I decided to be proactive. I spent a few hours drafting what I called a 'communications charter,' which I then proposed to my team leader before sharing it with the wider team. It wasn't revolutionary, but it set clear expectations: defined core working hours for communication, an agreement on expected response times (e.g., 24 hours for email, 2 hours for chat), and guidelines on when to use which tool—a phone call for anything urgent, for instance. To my relief, the idea was met with enthusiasm. It wasn't a panacea, but it was the first step in reclaiming our focus and well-being. The efficiency of the team has improved since, and more importantly, the collective anxiety has noticeably dropped.

THE DECLINE OF TRADITIONAL RETAIL

Over the past decade, the retail landscape has undergone dramatic transformation, with traditional brick-and-mortar stores struggling to maintain their foothold in the market. The rapid rise of e-commerce has fundamentally altered consumer behavior, with convenience, variety, and competitive pricing driving customers to online shopping platforms. While some retailers have adapted by embracing digital technologies, others have faltered, leading to the closure of countless high-street stores.

One significant factor contributing to this decline is the evolving expectations of consumers. Modern-day shoppers prioritize efficiency, often opting for the ability to browse and purchase items from the comfort of their homes. Same-day delivery and personalized marketing further enhance the appeal of online shopping. John Havers, a retail analyst, explains, "Today's consumers value immediacy and tailored experiences. Traditional retail, which often relies on outdated methods, struggles to keep pace with these demands."

Economic pressures also play a vital role. The cost of maintaining physical stores, including rent and employment, adds a financial burden that many businesses cannot sustain. By contrast, online retailers operate with much lower overheads. This disparity has created a fiercely competitive environment, with online giants often undercutting their traditional counterparts on price.

However, it would be premature to declare the death of the physical store. Many successful retailers are adopting a hybrid model, blending the strengths of online and offline commerce. For instance, the concept of "click-and-collect" allows customers to shop online and pick up their purchases in-store, combining convenience with immediacy. Additionally, some brands are leveraging their physical spaces to create immersive experiences, such as interactive displays and exclusive in-store events, which cannot be replicated online.

Still, challenges remain. The loss of retail jobs and the decline of bustling high streets have social and economic repercussions, particularly in smaller communities. Moreover, the environmental impact of e-commerce, including increased packaging waste and carbon emissions from delivery services, raises important sustainability concerns.

To survive in this evolving landscape, traditional retailers must rethink their strategies, embracing innovation while maintaining a sense of community. As Havers notes, "The future of retail lies not in resisting change but in finding ways to integrate the best of both worlds."

This means that brick-and-mortar stores need to blend digital convenience with personal, in-store experiences that online platforms cannot replicate. Investing in technologies such as augmented reality, personalized marketing, and seamless omnichannel systems can help retailers meet modern consumers’ expectations for speed and customization.

The caterpillar finds a safe spot and forms a protective casing around itself. This casing is called a chrysalis. Inside the (3), the caterpillar’s body completely transforms. It might look like nothing is happening from the outside, but a remarkable change is taking place.

After a period of time, which can be weeks or months, a beautiful butterfly breaks free from the casing. At first, its wings are soft and folded. The new (4) must pump fluid into its wings to make them strong enough for flight. After resting, the butterfly with its colorful (5) will fly away to drink nectar from flowers. This entire process of change is called metamorphosis, and it is one of nature’s most amazing wonders. Understanding (6) shows us how living things can adapt and change in extraordinary ways.

THE SCIENCE OF SLEEP

I. Sleep is a universal biological necessity, yet its precise mechanisms are still being explored. Far from being a passive state, sleep is a highly active period for the brain. It is governed by two main processes: the circadian rhythm, our internal 24-hour clock that tells us when to feel sleepy and when to be alert, and sleep pressure, which builds up the longer we are awake, creating a growing need for rest.

II. The architecture of sleep is complex, consisting of a recurring pattern of distinct phases. A typical night's sleep cycles between Non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) and Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep. NREM is further divided into three stages, progressing from light dozing to deep, restorative sleep. REM sleep, in contrast, is when the brain is highly active, breathing becomes irregular, and most vivid dreaming occurs. A full cycle through all stages takes approximately 90–110 minutes.

III. The reasons why we dedicate roughly a third of our lives to sleep are multifaceted. Physically, sleep is crucial for cellular repair, muscle growth, and the release of important hormones. Cognitively, it is indispensable for memory consolidation—the process by which recent learned experiences are transformed into long-term memory. It also allows the brain to clear out metabolic waste products that accumulate during waking hours.

IV. A chronic lack of sleep can have serious and wide-ranging consequences for health and well-being. In the short term, it leads to impaired concentration, poor decision-making, and mood swings. Over the long term, sleep deprivation is linked to an increased risk of significant health problems, including obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and a weakened immune system, making us more susceptible to infections.

V. Given its importance, cultivating good sleep hygiene is vital. Experts recommend maintaining a consistent sleep-wake schedule, even on weekends, to regulate the body's clock. Creating a relaxing bedtime routine, such as reading a book or taking a warm bath, can signal to the brain that it's time to wind down. It is also crucial to ensure the bedroom environment is dark, quiet, and cool, and to avoid stimulants like caffeine and electronic screens before bed.

VI. As people age, their sleep patterns often shift. Teenagers tend to fall asleep later and struggle to wake early, while older adults may become early risers and experience lighter, more fragmented sleep. These changes are influenced by hormonal variations and alterations in the body’s circadian rhythm. Understanding such natural shifts helps explain why sleep needs and habits vary across different stages of life.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

THE POWER OF SMELL

For most people, sight and hearing are the dominant senses, while smell is often considered less important. Yet research increasingly shows that our sense of smell plays a far greater role in daily life than we realise. From influencing our emotions and memories to shaping our social connections, scent can quietly guide our thoughts and behaviour in powerful ways.

The human nose can detect over a trillion different odours, although we are rarely conscious of this ability. When we encounter a familiar fragrance, it can instantly transport us to a specific moment in the past — a phenomenon known as “odor-evoked memory.” For example, the smell of fresh rain might remind someone of their childhood garden. Scientists have found that smells trigger more vivid and emotional memories than visual or auditory cues, partly because the olfactory system is directly linked to the brain’s limbic region, which processes emotions and memory.

In recent years, psychologists have explored how scent can affect mood and performance. One study discovered that people exposed to the smell of lavender became calmer and performed better on memory tests, while the scent of lemon made participants feel more alert. Retailers have even begun using this knowledge: a pleasant fragrance in a shop can subtly encourage customers to stay longer and spend more money. However, the effects of scent are not universal. A smell that one person finds soothing may be irritating to another, depending on personal associations and cultural background.

Interestingly, our ability to recognise and interpret smells can also influence social behaviour. Research suggests that people subconsciously use body odour to detect emotions such as fear or happiness in others. Some scientists believe that this hidden form of chemical communication evolved to help early humans survive by warning each other of danger or signalling trust. Despite these ancient roots, the modern world has largely masked natural body scents through perfumes and deodorants, reducing our awareness of this subtle form of interaction.

While smell has clear benefits, it can also cause problems. Individuals who lose their sense of smell — a condition known as anosmia — often report feelings of isolation or depression. Without the emotional richness that smells provide, many find that food becomes less enjoyable and that they struggle to recall certain memories. Fortunately, advances in neuroscience are helping researchers understand how to restore or strengthen olfactory function, offering hope to those affected.

Although we rarely stop to think about it, smell continues to shape our thoughts, decisions, and relationships in countless invisible ways. The next time a familiar aroma catches your attention, it might be worth pausing — your nose could be telling you more than you think.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

THE PARADOX OF CHOICE

In the modern world, consumers are surrounded by extraordinary abundance. Supermarkets, online platforms, and streaming services all promise endless possibilities — from thousands of breakfast cereals to millions of songs and movies. At first glance, this variety might appear to enhance personal freedom, giving people the ability to shape their experiences exactly as they wish. Yet psychologists argue that too many options can actually have the opposite effect. Instead of feeling liberated, individuals often become overwhelmed and stressed by the sheer number of decisions they must make each day.

The American psychologist Barry Schwartz introduced the term “the paradox of choice” to describe this phenomenon. His research suggests that when people face an excess of options, they experience decision fatigue and anxiety, often ending up less satisfied with their final choices. In one well-known experiment, shoppers presented with only six kinds of jam were far more likely to make a purchase than those offered twenty-four varieties. The conclusion was clear: a smaller number of choices makes decision-making both easier and more enjoyable.

However, not all scholars fully agree with Schwartz’s interpretation. Critics argue that the negative consequences of abundance depend largely on the context. For instance, individuals used to making complex decisions — such as investors, doctors, or managers — may actually thrive in environments with a wide range of alternatives. Others note that digital tools such as filters, search engines, and recommendation algorithms can simplify the process, allowing consumers to handle vast selections efficiently rather than feeling lost in them.

Cultural differences further complicate the picture. In some societies, the ability to choose freely is strongly associated with independence and personal identity, while in others, it is viewed as a potential source of pressure or confusion. Research shows that Western consumers often regard variety as empowering, whereas people from more collectivist cultures may prefer fewer, clearer choices. This suggests that the “paradox of choice” may not be a universal psychological truth, but rather a reflection of different cultural values and expectations.

Ultimately, the relationship between freedom and choice remains complex. Having multiple options can promote individuality and autonomy, yet an excess of them may undermine satisfaction and well-being. The challenge for modern societies is to strike the right balance — offering enough variety to support personal freedom without creating a sense of paralysis or discontent.

  • 15. Paragraph I

I. The Native Americans were the first known inhabitants of the Americas and are often described as the world’s first environmentalists. To them, every part of nature — animal, plant, or stone — possessed a spirit and deserved respect. They took what they needed from the land but never more than necessary, showing deep gratitude for nature’s gifts. Their traditions taught that harming the earth would ultimately harm the people themselves, creating a strong sense of balance and responsibility toward the environment.

II. Native Americans lived in many different regions, yet the exact origins of their ancestors remain uncertain. Some believe they have always lived on the continent since the beginning of time. Others argue that their ancestors migrated from Asia thousands of years ago, crossing the Bering Strait Land Bridge. Although many theories exist, none have been definitively proven. Modern DNA studies continue to explore these questions, revealing that the genetic history of Native peoples is far more complex than once imagined.

III. When Christopher Columbus arrived in the Americas, he mistakenly believed he had reached India. As a result, he called the native inhabitants “Indians,” a name that — despite being incorrect — became permanent. In reality, there were numerous independent tribes, each with unique languages, traditions, and beliefs. Nevertheless, the collective term “Indians” persisted for centuries. Even today, the debate continues over which term — “Native American,” “Indigenous,” or “First Nations” — best reflects their true identity and heritage.

IV. When the Pilgrims arrived on the Mayflower in 1620 seeking religious freedom, they were warmly received by a local tribe in Massachusetts. The Native Americans shared food, farming knowledge, and hunting techniques, teaching the newcomers how to survive in the unfamiliar environment. The holiday of Thanksgiving still commemorates this early act of kindness and cooperation. Without such guidance, the settlers might not have survived their first harsh winter in the New World.

V. Sadly, this peaceful coexistence did not last long. Native Americans had no immunity to European diseases such as smallpox, measles, and typhus. As settlers spread across the land, these illnesses devastated indigenous populations. It is estimated that in some tribes, up to ninety percent of people died within a century of European contact — a tragedy beyond measure. The loss of so many lives also meant the disappearance of languages, stories, and cultural traditions that could never be recovered.

VI. As European colonization expanded, the situation for Native Americans worsened. Many were deceived into signing treaties after being given alcohol, or simply forced off their ancestral lands through violence. They were eventually confined to reservations — areas that were often barren and unfit for farming. Through lies and force, much of their territory was taken from them forever. Generations later, the struggle for land rights and cultural recognition continues to shape Native American life and identity.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

A MAN OF SCIENCE AND IMAGINATION

Sir Christopher Wren was one of the most remarkable figures of 17th-century England — a scientist, mathematician, astronomer, inventor, and ultimately, one of the country’s greatest architects. Born in 1632 into a wealthy and educated family, he was a rather fragile child who received private lessons from tutors and his father at home. Wren’s early education remains somewhat uncertain, as there are no records confirming whether he attended any formal school. However, historical sources show that in 1650 he entered Oxford University, where he studied mathematics and natural philosophy — what we now call science.

After completing his studies, Wren became a Professor of Astronomy at Gresham College in London. He was responsible for delivering weekly speeches in both Latin and English, which were open to anyone free of charge. His lectures attracted great attention and led to the creation of the Royal Society — the first official scientific organization in England. Later, he also taught at Oxford, where he continued his research in many areas, including optics, mechanics, medicine, and meteorology. Always curious, Wren designed and improved various devices and machines, experimenting with submarine construction, telescope design, and road paving techniques.

During this period, Wren’s interests gradually expanded from science to architecture. In the 17th century, the job of “architect” was not yet recognized as a formal profession. Important buildings were usually designed according to the patron’s wishes and executed by skilled craftsmen such as carpenters and masons. For well-educated gentlemen like Wren, architecture was considered more of a refined hobby than a career. Nevertheless, his extraordinary talent quickly gained recognition. After the Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed much of the city, Wren was entrusted with the massive task of rebuilding many of its churches. In total, he designed 51 London churches — including his masterpiece, St Paul’s Cathedral — each one distinctive yet sharing a classical elegance. His attention to detail and insistence on high-quality materials set new standards for English architecture. Wren was knighted in 1673 in recognition of his exceptional contributions.

The construction of St Paul’s Cathedral began in 1675 when Wren was 43 years old. Blending elements of Medieval, Classical, and Baroque design, it remains a symbol of London’s resilience and beauty. Its enormous dome and breathtaking interior demonstrate both scientific precision and artistic vision. The project took 35 years to complete, and fittingly, the final stone was laid by Wren’s son.

Today, St Paul’s Cathedral remains an active place of worship as well as a national landmark. Over the centuries, it has hosted numerous significant events — from the funerals of Lord Nelson and Sir Winston Churchill to services marking the end of both World Wars. More recently, it has been the site of royal celebrations, including the Queen’s jubilees and birthdays.

Sir Christopher Wren passed away on February 25th, 1723, at the age of 90. He was buried in St Paul’s Cathedral, the very building he had created. His gravestone bears a Latin inscription that translates: “If you seek his monument, look around you.” It reminds visitors that his true memorial is not a statue or a plaque — but the magnificent work that still stands above London today.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

THE SCIENCE OF HAPPINESS

Happiness is something that every culture values, yet it remains one of life’s biggest mysteries. Around the world, people pursue success, wealth, and love in their search for lasting joy — but scientific research suggests that true happiness depends not only on what we achieve, but also on how we think, behave, and connect with others.

Scientists describe happiness as a blend of joy, calmness, and life satisfaction. It can originate from simple pleasures — like sharing a meal with friends, watching a sunset, or laughing at a funny story — as well as from greater accomplishments. However, happiness is not just a short-lived feeling; it’s also a state of mind. Some people naturally focus on the positive aspects of life, while others find it harder to maintain that emotional balance.

Psychologists and neuroscientists have found that our brains play a crucial role in how happy we feel. When people experience positive emotions, their brains unleash chemicals like dopamine and serotonin, which are linked to delight, motivation, and eased pressure. Activities such as exercise, laughter, listening to music, or even spending time in nature can increase these chemicals, improving our overall mood and mental well-being.

It is fascinating that happiness is not determined solely by external circumstances or the possessions we own. Our mindset and everyday behaviors also play a crucial role in shaping it. Individuals who make gratitude a consistent part of their lives—by acknowledging what they value or noting down the positives—often experience greater overall well-being. Likewise, people who cultivate optimistic thoughts and treat themselves with kindness tend to handle stress more effectively and maintain stronger emotional balance.

Research indicates that individuals who maintain strong bonds—whether with loved ones, friends, or even animals—tend to enjoy better health, greater life satisfaction, and increased longevity. Kindness also has a remarkable influence. Engaging in helpful acts, volunteering, or showing generosity triggers the release of chemicals in the brain that elevate mood, a reaction often referred to as the helper’s high. Even simple actions, such as a smile or a thoughtful word, can leave a surprisingly positive and lasting effect.

Money, too, affects happiness — but only to a certain extent. Financial security and the ability to meet basic needs such as food, housing, and safety are essential for peace of mind. However, once those needs are met, earning more money brings only a small increase in long-term satisfaction. In fact, people who focus too much on wealth or possessions often end up feeling less fulfilled. Experiences — like travelling, learning something new, or spending time with loved ones — usually bring deeper and more lasting happiness than material things.

Finally, happiness doesn’t mean being cheerful every moment of the day. Everyone experiences sadness, anger, or stress from time to time. What matters is how we deal with those emotions. Practices such as mindfulness — paying attention to the present moment — along with good sleep, healthy eating, and regular exercise can all help us maintain a positive outlook and a sense of balance in our lives.

PART 3Questions 15–20

Read the text and choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below. There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use all of them. You cannot use any heading more than once.

LIST OF HEADINGS:
  • A) The ways in which laws preserve order and safeguard society
  • B) How new laws are designed and passed into action
  • C) Varied structures of global legal frameworks
  • D) The earliest emergence of recorded legal codes
  • E) Outcomes faced by individuals who violate laws
  • F) Reforming laws to uphold justice and equality
  • G) Debates over the length of certain punishment periods
  • H) The principal divisions within legal systems
  • 15. Paragraph I
  • 16. Paragraph II
  • 17. Paragraph III
  • 18. Paragraph IV
  • 19. Paragraph V
  • 20. Paragraph VI

THE ROLE OF LAWS IN MODERN SOCIETY

I. Every society requires a clear set of guidelines to operate smoothly. These guidelines, called laws, direct how individuals should act. Laws define what behavior is acceptable and what is not. Their main purpose is to safeguard people, resolve conflicts, and ensure public security. For instance, traffic regulations help prevent accidents, while criminal laws stop theft and violence. Without laws, citizens might feel unsafe, and communities could quickly fall into chaos and disorder.

II. The idea of creating laws is not new. Thousands of years ago, ancient civilizations began developing written codes of conduct. One of the earliest known examples is the Code of Hammurabi from Babylon, which detailed specific punishments for various offenses. This reveals that even ancient people valued justice and fairness. Later, Roman law became more advanced and has greatly influenced modern legal systems, especially throughout Europe and other regions shaped by Roman traditions.

III. In most countries today, new rules start as proposals written by elected lawmakers. These representatives discuss, debate, and often revise them before taking a vote. If a majority supports the proposal, it officially becomes a law. Afterward, courts and judges interpret and apply these laws to actual situations. In democratic nations, ordinary citizens can also participate by signing petitions, joining advocacy groups, or voting for leaders who share their views on justice.

IV. Laws do not all serve the same function. Criminal laws address crimes such as robbery, fraud, or assault. Civil laws handle disagreements between people, such as property issues or contract breaches. Family laws deal with matters like marriage, divorce, and child custody, while environmental laws aim to protect nature. Traffic laws help maintain safety on the roads. Dividing the law into these categories allows governments to manage society’s complexity more clearly and fairly.

V. Anyone who breaks the law faces consequences. These can include paying fines, losing a license, doing community service, or, for serious crimes, going to prison. The severity of punishment depends on the seriousness of the offense. Courts are responsible for ensuring that penalties are fair and consistent. Yet, public debates often arise — some argue that certain punishments are too harsh, while others believe they are too lenient.

VI. For any legal system to function effectively, its laws must be fair, flexible, and adaptable. When rules are unjust, people may lose faith in their government, leading to protests or defiance. Strong laws protect all citizens, especially those who are vulnerable or belong to minority groups, and they must evolve with time. Modern issues such as cybercrime, digital privacy, and climate change demand new and updated legislation. A successful legal system must balance tradition and innovation to keep society both safe and fair for everyone.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

TINY CREATURES, MIGHTY INFLUENCE

Insects are the most abundant and varied group of animals on Earth. They inhabit nearly every environment imaginable — from humid rainforests and scorching deserts to icy mountaintops and dark underground caves. Some even share our living spaces, feeding on our food and nesting in our homes. Experts estimate that there may be over ten million species of insects worldwide, although only around one million have been formally described. Statistically, for every single person, there could exist over 200 million insects. Their hidden world is vast, intricate, and endlessly fascinating.

Despite their diversity, all insects share a number of unique physical traits. Each insect’s body consists of three sections — the head, thorax, and abdomen — and features six legs and a pair of antennae. Many insects have wings, which help them to travel, locate mates, or escape predators. Yet not all species can fly; ants and fleas, for instance, lack wings but are still perfectly suited to their environments. Insects belong to the wider animal group known as arthropods, which also includes spiders, crabs, and centipedes. However, unlike their relatives, insects always possess six legs and a three-part body design, setting them apart within the animal kingdom.

Insects perform indispensable tasks within ecosystems. Bees, for example, pollinate nearly one-third of all the food humans consume. Without their activity — and that of other pollinators — the reproduction of many fruits, vegetables, and flowers would be severely disrupted. Ants contribute by cleaning their habitats, feeding on dead organisms and leftover food, helping to prevent the spread of disease. Butterflies and moths, admired for their elegance, also assist in pollination while enriching natural landscapes with color. Farmers often rely on ladybirds, which feed on pests such as aphids that damage harvests. Because of these small but vital creatures, many plants thrive without excessive dependence on chemical pesticides.

Life is not easy for insects, and survival demands creativity. Over time, they have developed remarkable defensive mechanisms. Some camouflage themselves to match leaves or bark, while others display bright warning colors like red, orange, or yellow to signal toxicity. Beetles protect themselves with hard shells, whereas flies depend on rapid flight to escape danger. Certain species release unpleasant smells or painful stings as chemical weapons. Communication is also crucial for safety — ants leave chemical trails to guide their nestmates to food, and crickets rub their wings together to produce rhythmic chirps that attract mates or claim territory.

Perhaps the most intriguing feature of insects is their life cycle. Most undergo metamorphosis, progressing through four stages — egg, larva, pupa, and adult. Take the butterfly as an example: it begins as an egg, transforms into a caterpillar, becomes a chrysalis, and finally emerges as an adult butterfly. This process enables insects to inhabit different environments and functions throughout life. Some species, such as dragonflies, begin their existence underwater before taking flight as adults — a clear demonstration of their extraordinary adaptability.

Many insects also show impressive levels of social organization. While some live solitary lives, others — including ants, bees, and termites — form highly structured colonies. These societies are divided into distinct castes: workers, soldiers, and queens, each with specialized duties. Workers gather food, soldiers defend, and queens reproduce. Such cooperation allows colonies to survive even under extreme conditions. Scientists often liken these communities to human cities, as both rely heavily on teamwork, communication, and shared purpose.

Insects are not only vital to nature but also essential to human existence. They recycle nutrients, pollinate crops, and serve as food sources for birds, reptiles, and fish. Without them, entire ecosystems would collapse, and human agriculture would face catastrophic losses. Yet insect populations are rapidly declining due to pollution, habitat destruction, and climate change. Safeguarding these small creatures is therefore critical — not merely for their survival, but for the stability of the planet and humanity itself.

Although they may seem insignificant, insects are among the most successful species ever to inhabit Earth. Their capacity to adapt, cooperate, and contribute makes them truly exceptional. They remind us that even the tiniest beings can leave the largest mark on our world.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

A NEW GIANT IN THE SKY

In the misty mountains of Guizhou Province, China, a new engineering wonder now stretches across the deep Huajiang Canyon. On Sunday, the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge officially opened to the public — instantly becoming the tallest bridge in the world, rising an astonishing 625 metres above the Beipan River. The project represents not only a record-breaking height but also remarkable technological progress. The bridge extends a total of 2,890 metres, with a main span of 1,420 metres, making it the longest bridge ever built in such steep and challenging terrain. It is widely viewed as one of the most advanced constructions of its kind anywhere on Earth.

For people living in the region, the bridge is far more than just a symbol of progress — it’s a practical lifeline. Before it was built, drivers had to take a winding two-hour journey to cross the river. Now, thanks to the bridge, that same trip takes barely two minutes. This dramatic reduction in travel time allows local people to reach schools, hospitals, and workplaces much more easily. Transporting goods such as food, medicine, and building materials has also become far faster and cheaper. Businesses can grow more efficiently, families can stay connected, and rural areas can integrate better with nearby cities. A government official stated that the bridge would “inject new economic energy into the region” by linking isolated areas with major trade routes.

China’s achievements in bridge construction are attracting global attention. According to highestbridges.com, the 18 tallest bridges in the world are all located in China — either already completed or still under construction. Experts say this success proves the country’s growing leadership in large-scale infrastructure and engineering innovation.

Building the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge was no simple task. Engineers had to overcome dangerous winds, high altitudes, and extremely steep cliffs. To ensure safety, they equipped the bridge with special wind-resistant systems that allow it to remain stable during storms or bad weather. Advanced technology was used to lift and position materials across the deep canyon, requiring extraordinary precision and teamwork. Engineers around the world now study this bridge as a model of what can be achieved when human skill meets determination.

However, the bridge’s significance extends far beyond transportation and industrial value. It has evolved into a major destination for tourists, capturing attention with its magnificent scenery. Authorities anticipate that the site will welcome a huge number of tourists annually. To accommodate them, a modern visitor centre has been established, featuring a café, a geological museum that illustrates how the canyon was formed, and even a bungee-jumping platform designed for adventure enthusiasts seeking an adrenaline rush.

In a broader sense, the bridge represents China’s transformation over the past few decades. Once, many rural regions were isolated with little access to modern transport. Today, the country is home to the tallest bridges, the fastest trains, and some of the world’s most ambitious engineering projects. The Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge is more than a structure — it’s a symbol of how quickly innovation can reshape a nation.

7. www.greenroute.org
Planning a trip soon? This site calculates how much fuel or electricity various types of transport use. Assess trains, planes, and cars to see which option leaves the smallest carbon footprint. There’s also a short guide on eco-friendly travel habits. A new feature even lets users analyze routes to see how weather conditions affect energy use.
8. www.natureconnect.org
An online platform where volunteers can find nearby projects such as planting trees, collecting litter, or helping in wildlife reserves. Users can share stories and photos from their experiences to encourage others to take part. Monthly challenges reward the most active members with eco-friendly prizes.
9. www.futureenergy.co.uk
If you want to learn how wind, water, and sunlight can power our homes and cities, this website explains everything clearly. Interactive maps show which countries are switching from oil and gas to renewable energy. It also includes interviews with engineers developing next-generation solar panels.
10. www.askascientist.net
Want to know what experts are discovering about the planet? Here you can read blog posts written by scientists and even send them your own requests. They reply to selected ones each week, making complex topics easy to understand. A podcast series is also available where specialists discuss their latest environmental studies.
11. www.homeecoideas.com
From saving water to reducing waste, this site gives practical advice for anyone who wants to live more sustainably. There are videos about turning off unused devices, growing your own herbs, and choosing energy-efficient lighting. Visitors can download a free checklist to track their weekly progress at home.
12. www.rethinkdesign.org
Discover creative ways to redesign materials that might otherwise be thrown away. You’ll find tutorials on making furniture from cardboard or bags from torn jeans — proof that sustainability can be stylish too! New community challenges invite users to share photos of their own upcycled creations.
13. www.cleanplate.org
Did you know that what we eat influences the earth’s health? Learn about how reducing meat, avoiding food waste, and buying local produce can lower your carbon footprint. Includes recipes from environmentally conscious chefs. A calculator also estimates how much water and land you save with each plant-based meal.
14. www.ecostyleworld.com
Stay up-to-date with fashion that doesn’t harm the planet. This site reviews brands that use recycled fabrics or pay fair wages to their workers. There’s also advice on how to shop responsibly and care for clothes to make them last longer. Its monthly blog highlights new designers creating eco-friendly collections worldwide.

DISCOVERING THE SAFARI EXPERIENCE

I. A safari traditionally refers to a journey through untamed land — most often in vast grasslands or dense jungles — undertaken to observe or hunt wild animals. Historically, safaris were primarily hunting expeditions organized by wealthy Europeans seeking trophies such as lion skins or elephant tusks. Over the decades, however, this perception has dramatically evolved. Today, most safaris are centred on viewing and photographing animals rather than harming them. The rise of wildlife protection laws and global concern about endangered species has led to a new, ethical approach where the aim is to witness wildlife in its natural state, not to conquer it. Modern safaris therefore represent both an adventure and a conscious act of preservation.

II. The term safari originates from the Swahili language but can be traced even further back to the Arabic verb safara, meaning to travel. While Africa remains the birthplace and spiritual home of the safari tradition, the concept has expanded across continents. Today, safari adventures can be found not only in the savannas of Kenya or Tanzania but also among the dense jungles of India, the icy landscapes of Antarctica, the arid outback of Australia, or the lush rainforests of the Amazon Basin. In Alaska and Canada, too, guided wildlife tours have become increasingly popular. In essence, any destination where animals roam freely and humans are temporary guests can be described as a safari.

III. Although the idea of trekking through the wilderness on foot sounds thrilling, it is often safer to observe animals from a secure vehicle or protected viewpoint. Predators such as lions, tigers, or bears may appear calm at a distance, but their unpredictable instincts can make close human encounters life-threatening. Likewise, frequent intrusion by humans may distress animals or disrupt their feeding patterns. For this reason, many safaris rely on jeeps, minibuses, or even specially designed observation trucks. From within these vehicles, visitors can admire wildlife at close range while remaining safely shielded. This approach ensures both the safety of travellers and the wellbeing of the animals, maintaining the delicate balance between curiosity and conservation.

IV. The duration and style of a safari can vary greatly. Some tours last a mere weekend, while others extend over several weeks, traversing vast regions by plane, jeep, or even hot-air balloon. Many itineraries include camping beneath the stars or staying in eco-lodges near wildlife reserves. Because safaris often involve multiple locations and transport changes, travellers are advised to take only essentials. Overpacking can become a serious inconvenience on budget or mobile safaris, where every kilogram counts. A compact backpack, comfortable clothing, and essential gear such as binoculars and insect repellent are far more valuable than heavy suitcases.

V. Africa remains the ultimate safari places, with Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, and Botswana drawing millions of visitors each year. Yet, the allure of safari travel extends well beyond this continent. Australia offers unique outback tours featuring kangaroos and emus, while India’s national parks are home to Bengal tigers and elephants. In South America, the rainforests of Brazil and Peru provide opportunities to observe monkeys, parrots, and river dolphins in their natural habitats. Meanwhile, in Alaska, visitors can witness the raw beauty of grizzly bears fishing for salmon or watch polar bears wandering along icy shores. Many of these excursions combine multiple experiences — such as cruises, treks, or photography workshops — making the modern safari a global and highly diverse phenomenon.

VI. Closely related to the safari experience is the concept of eco-adventure — a form of travel that emphasizes sustainability, education, and respect for nature. An eco-adventure might involve canoeing along the Amazon River, hiking through tropical rainforests, or joining a conservation-based safari in Africa. These journeys encourage travellers to engage with local communities, learn about fragile ecosystems, and minimize their environmental footprint. Responsible tour operators ensure that participants follow “leave no trace” principles and often contribute financially to local conservation projects. In this way, eco-adventure tourism transforms ordinary sightseeing into a purposeful journey that benefits both people and the planet.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

THE HIDDEN WORLD BENEATH THE SEA

The ocean covers more than seventy percent of the Earth’s surface, yet much of it remains an untouched mystery. Scientists estimate that over eighty percent of the world’s seas and oceans have never been properly explored or mapped. In other words, most of our planet’s largest ecosystem is still hidden from view. Within this immense, dark, and shifting realm lie countless secrets — from strange life forms and unexplained natural sounds to puzzling underwater structures and phenomena that science has only begun to understand. The deep ocean, in many ways, is like another planet — unfamiliar, dangerous, and full of extraordinary surprises waiting to be revealed.

One of the most enigmatic areas of the ocean is the deep-sea floor. This vast region exists in total darkness, where the pressure is so immense that humans cannot survive without specially designed equipment. Because of this, exploration relies heavily on advanced submersibles, underwater robots, and remote sensors. Despite decades of research, oceanographers admit that humanity still knows more about the surface of Mars than about our own seabed. What lies beneath the waves includes underwater mountain ranges, enormous trenches deeper than Everest is tall, and even volcanoes that continue to erupt unseen. In some regions, strange shapes and formations resemble man-made buildings or pyramids. Near Japan, for example, lies the Yonaguni Monument, a mysterious underwater structure. Some claim it is the remains of an ancient civilization swallowed by the sea, while others insist it is simply the product of natural erosion.

The ocean’s mysteries are not only visual but also auditory. The sea is full of sounds, many of which are still unexplained. Perhaps the most famous example is “The Bloop”, a powerful low-frequency noise recorded in 1997. When it was first heard, it sparked speculation that it came from a gigantic, unknown sea creature lurking in the depths. Later studies suggested it might instead have been produced by the fracturing of icebergs, though no one has ever proved this conclusively. Similar strange noises — deep rumbles, eerie clicks, or metallic echoes — continue to puzzle scientists, who are still trying to identify their sources.

Equally fascinating is the mysterious “milky sea” phenomenon, in which vast sections of the ocean surface suddenly begin to glow with a pale blue or white light. Sailors have reported this event for centuries, describing entire horizons illuminated as if by moonlight. Modern researchers believe that this glow is caused by bioluminescent bacteria that emit light when they gather in huge colonies, although the exact process that allows such vast gatherings to occur remains unclear. Remarkably, some of these glowing seas are so extensive that satellites orbiting the Earth have captured them from space.

Beneath the waves lies a realm teeming with life — much of it unlike anything found on land. Creatures that dwell thousands of metres below the surface have adapted to an environment of perpetual darkness and crushing pressure. Many possess bizarre shapes, translucent skin, or the ability to generate their own light. Some have no eyes at all, while others display features that seem to belong in science fiction rather than reality. Every deep-sea expedition yields new species, suggesting that our catalog of marine life is far from complete. In fact, the ocean may still hold countless organisms we have yet to encounter — each one revealing something new about the possibilities of life on Earth.

The ocean has long captured human imagination not only because of what lives in it but also because of what has disappeared within it. The Bermuda Triangle, a region of the Atlantic Ocean between Florida, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico, has become famous for mysterious vanishings of ships and aircraft. Over the years, countless theories have been proposed — from supernatural forces and magnetic disturbances to unpredictable weather patterns and navigational errors. While most scientists agree that ordinary explanations such as storms or human mistakes are the most likely causes, the legend continues to fuel curiosity about what really happens in that enigmatic part of the sea.

Though science has revealed parts of the ocean, most of it remains unexplored. Its depths may hold clues to Earth’s past, new medicines, energy sources, and the origins of life. As technology improves, researchers aim to explore further — not just out of curiosity, but to understand and protect this vast, mysterious world.
