PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

THE FIFTH TASTE

When we were young, many of us learnt that there are four basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. However, scientists now say there is a fifth taste: umami. Unlike the other four, umami is more subtle and complex, often described as a deep, savory, or meaty flavor. While it may not be as immediately recognizable as sweetness or sourness, it plays a crucial role in enhancing the overall taste experience of many dishes. From rich broths and aged cheeses to ripe tomatoes and cured meats, umami is present in a wide range of foods, adding depth and satisfaction to every bite.

Umami, which has been enjoyed by Eastern countries for centuries, was recently brought to people’s attention in the West by scientists at the University of Miami in the US. The word ‘umami’ is new to many people, but not to the Japanese, who’ve used it since the early 1900s to describe the fifth taste. So, what exactly is the umami taste? Well, there’s no word in English which means the same, and it’s often described as a savory or meaty taste.

Recognizing the umami taste takes practice; it’s not as obvious as the other tastes. For example, when eating a homemade chicken soup made without salt or pepper, most people would find it too plain. Adding a small amount of something called ‘monosodium glutamate’ to that same soup gives it the umami taste and would probably lead you to say that the soup now tastes more like chicken soup than it did before. It’s not as simple as making something more salty, as salt alone can do that. Instead, the umami taste is one of richness and fullness. Basically, it just makes the food taste more delicious.

Asian cooks began adding seaweed – a type of plant from the sea – to soups over 1,200 years ago. They’d discovered that foods cooked with seaweed simply tasted better. They didn’t know, however, that the reason for this improved flavor was actually the high levels of glutamate which exist naturally in the seaweed.

Eventually, in 1908, a Japanese scientist made the connection between glutamate and seaweed. He then studied the various kinds of glutamate, trying to find one that gave the umami taste, and that could also be produced in factories. He found that the sodium salt form, called monosodium glutamate, was exactly what he was looking for. It provided umami, and it was easy for cooks to use and store. Monosodium glutamate, usually called ‘MSG’, was first produced in Japan in 1909. Since then, it has been used by food producers and home cooks to improve the flavor of a wide variety of dishes.

So, which foods naturally contain glutamate? Well, meats, cheese and other high-protein foods have a lot of glutamate. In some, the amount of glutamate they contain, and their flavor, increases as they get older. For example, old cheese has more glutamate than young cheese and this also happens with some vegetables, like tomatoes. This is why a red tomato tastes much better than a green one. Think about that the next time you make a sandwich or a salad!

Interestingly, umami is not only about enhancing flavor—it also plays a crucial role in nutrition. Scientists believe that our ability to detect umami evolved as a way to recognize protein-rich foods, which are essential for muscle growth and overall health. When we eat umami-rich foods, they stimulate our appetite and digestion, making us more likely to consume the nutrients our bodies need. Additionally, umami can make low-salt dishes taste more satisfying, which is why it’s often used as a healthier alternative to excessive salt in cooking. This makes umami not just a fascinating taste but also an important part of a balanced diet.

INTERNATIONAL INVENTIONS

Do you use paper every day? Or check the time on your watch? These everyday things weren’t always part of life. Many of the (1) we depend on today actually come from many different parts of the world.

Paper, for example, was first made in ancient China more than two thousand years ago. It was invented by a man named Cai Lun, who used tree bark and old cloth to make thin sheets. From (2), the idea spread along trade routes to the Middle East and then to Europe. Without this discovery, reading and writing would have been much more difficult!

The wrist watch has its roots in Europe. The first small, portable clocks were made in Germany in the 1500s, and people started to wear them on their (3) about 300 years later. Today, watches not only tell the (4) but can also track our health and show messages.

And what about chocolate? It originally came from Central America, where the (5) Mayans and Aztecs drank it as a bitter liquid. When Spanish explorers brought cocoa beans to Europe, people added sugar to this (6) in order to make it sweeter. Now, chocolate is one of the most loved treats around the world.

Each of these items—paper, watches, and chocolate—shows how ideas travel and change. It’s amazing how inventions from long ago shape our daily lives today.

7. WanderWise Adventures
We organise active hiking and cycling holidays for people who love being outdoors. Our most popular tours include climbing routes in Spain and mountain biking in Italy. Want to improve your shooting skills while seeing the world? Our professional instructors will teach you how to take great nature shots in national parks and along the coast. 10. SoloPlan

Ideal for travellers who prefer elegance and comfort. Each itinerary is tailored to your interests, from art to gastronomy.

THE KINGDOM TOWER

I. Work has just started on the new Kingdom Tower in the coastal city of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Its developers say it will be the tallest building in the world when it has been completed. Not only that, the Tower will also have the world’s fastest and highest double-decker elevator. The building is expected to take five years to complete and will be ready by 2019 at the latest.

II. The idea behind the project belongs to a member of the Saudi royal family, Prince Al Waleed bin Talal. The prince envisions that this project will make Saudi Arabia — particularly Jeddah — a global highlight and boost its international trade and business connections. He also hopes that the project will provide hundreds of jobs for the people of Saudi Arabia.

III. The Kingdom Tower will measure 1 km. This is 173 meters taller than the current world record holder, Dubai’s Burj Khalifa standing at 827 meters, and four times taller than The Shard in London, which is currently the tallest building in Western Europe. It is estimated that the building will cost $1.23 billion, using approximately 530,000 square meters of concrete and 80,000 tons of steel for its 200 floors. It will have a five-star hotel, apartments, office space and an observatory – a room from where people can watch the planets and stars – as well as amazing views of the Red Sea.

IV. The Jeddah Economic Company (JEC), which is responsible for building the Kingdom Tower, says the building will have a total of 59 elevators, including five that are double. These have a travel speed of over 10 meters per second and will take visitors to the observatory. Speaking for JEC, Mounib Hammoud said they plan to work with elevator company Kone because they have the best technology in the business. This means that elevators can travel to heights that are twice the distance that was previously possible, while still being environmentally friendly.

V. However, building a tower of this height is not simple. Because it is near the salt water of the sea, it is extremely important that the correct building materials are used. Wind can also be a problem for such a tall building, but the architects have found a solution. One of them, Gordon Gill, explains that ‘because it changes shape every few floors, the wind loads go round the building and won’t be as extreme as on a solid block.’

VI. A special team of technical advisers has also been employed on the project to ensure the highest standards of quality and safety. The Advanced Construction Technology Services Company is actively involved in experimenting and analyzing the materials required for constructing the tower. Their role includes assessing the durability, strength, and environmental impact of the materials to ensure they meet industry standards and regulatory requirements. Additionally, they provide expert recommendations on innovative building techniques and cutting-edge construction solutions to enhance the tower’s structural integrity and sustainability.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

THE BENEFITS OF BOREDOM

Nowadays, wherever you look, it’s normal to see people plugged into various electronic devices such as smartphones and tablets. This information overload, designed to stimulate our minds and keep us distracted, seems like a very modern-day matter, but it isn’t. One unique thinker addressed a similar issue over seventy years ago: radical, or extreme boredom. In 1942, a German writer called Siegfried Kracauer described how city life provided people with too many things that kept their minds occupied. And he suggested we should cut ourselves off for controlled periods to experience ‘extraordinary, radical boredom’. On pleasant afternoons when everyone else was outside, he recommended instead that people should stay at home, draw the curtains and do nothing whatsoever on the sofa.

Kracauer believed that actively practicing boredom was a valuable means of unlocking playful wild ideas far away from plain reality. It’s a beautiful theory and one that would definitely appeal to many people, and modern research suggests that it might actually have a strong psychological basis.

To test the potential benefits of boredom, psychologist Dr Sandi Mann asked a group of forty people to complete a task designed to demonstrate their creativity. But before they started the task, a smaller group of people from this larger group was asked to perform a suitably dull task – copying numbers from the telephone directory for 15 minutes. The results of the overall test suggested that the smaller group that had done the boring task actually displayed more creative talent than those who hadn’t done it. According to psychologists, when people become bored and start to daydream about being on holiday in an exotic location or being rich, for instance, their minds use different processes which can help them work out more creative solutions to problems.

This might suggest then, that by keeping our minds continuously busy, we’re not just making ourselves more stressed, we’re also missing out on a chance to separate our thoughts from daily routines and to think more creatively. Psychologists explain that despite its bad reputation, boredom has a definite purpose. Mann says that without it, we’d be like very young children in a constant state of amazement at the world around us. Mann further points out that we shouldn’t teach small children that boredom and lack of stimulation are things to be feared rather than welcomed.

So how should we learn to get used to periods of radical boredom? The first step is realizing that it’s different from simply taking time to think about what you’ve done since getting up that morning. Mann explains that we can use boredom positively by creating opportunities when our minds aren’t occupied. This could be just staring out of the window or watching the rain. Anything that allows you to lose concentration is beneficial, according to Mann – a bit like taking a holiday from your brain!

Furthermore, embracing boredom can also improve mental well-being by reducing stress and anxiety. In today's fast-paced world, where people are constantly bombarded with notifications and deadlines, moments of boredom provide a rare opportunity for relaxation and introspection. Studies suggest that allowing the mind to wander freely can enhance problem-solving skills and emotional resilience. Instead of viewing boredom as an inconvenience, experts argue that it should be seen as a necessary mental reset—one that helps individuals regain focus, boost productivity, and cultivate a deeper sense of mindfulness in their daily lives.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

HIGH PRICE OF PROGRESS

Throughout history, human progress has often been celebrated as a triumph of intelligence and ambition. New inventions have allowed us to live longer, travel faster, and communicate instantly across the planet. Yet, every major leap forward has also brought its own set of dangers and ethical questions. The debate over how much risk society should tolerate in the name of progress remains unresolved, especially in an age when technological change happens faster than ever before.

The Industrial Revolution, for example, transformed economies and improved living standards for millions. But it also introduced several serious safety issues such as factory pollution, dangerous working conditions, and the exploitation of child labor. At the time, few questioned these consequences because industrialization promised growth and national power. In hindsight, we can see that the benefits were undeniable, but so were the costs. Similar patterns continue today in the digital age, where convenience often overshadows caution.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the clearest examples of this dilemma. Supporters argue that AI can revolutionize medicine, transportation, and education by performing tasks faster and with more accuracy than humans. Yet, critics warn of serious dangers — from job losses to privacy violations, and even the possibility that machines could make harmful decisions without human control. Calls for stronger ethical regulation are often dismissed by those who fear that too much caution could slow innovation. The question, then, is not whether we should develop AI, but rather how to do so responsibly.

Some economists compare this situation to the early years of nuclear energy. When nuclear power was first developed, it was praised as a clean, efficient alternative to coal and oil. Few people imagined it would also lead to catastrophic accidents like Chernobyl or Fukushima, or that the same science could be used to create weapons of mass destruction. Advocates of progress often insist that the potential benefits outweigh the risks, but this argument assumes that human beings are capable of managing those risks perfectly — something history repeatedly disproves.

Nevertheless, a complete rejection of risk is neither realistic nor productive. Without taking risks, humanity would never have discovered vaccines, electricity, or the internet. What is needed is not blind fear or blind faith, but a middle path — a method of making informed decisions about risk. This means weighing the probable benefits against the potential harm, while ensuring that the people affected by new technologies have a voice in deciding whether they should be adopted.

Public awareness also plays a vital role. Many of the problems associated with new technology arise not from the inventions themselves, but from how they are used or misunderstood. For instance, social media was originally designed to connect people, yet it has contributed to misinformation and mental health issues. Similarly, genetic editing could cure diseases but might also be misused to create “designer babies.” In each case, society must decide whether the moral and social costs justify the advantages.

Ultimately, progress is not a single direction but a balance between innovation and responsibility. The more powerful our technologies become, the more humility we need in applying them. History suggests that true progress is not defined by how quickly we advance, but by how wisely we choose to move forward.

THE POWER OF MUSIC

I. From ancient tribal drums echoing through forests to today’s digital pop hits, music has always been an inseparable part of human civilization. Every society, regardless of its size or isolation, has produced its own forms of musical expression. This universality suggests that music is far more than a form of amusement — it is a vital channel for sharing feelings, preserving stories, and building connections among people. Even when listeners do not understand the lyrics, they can still sense the tone and emotion behind a melody. Music functions as a shared language of emotion, transcending cultural and linguistic barriers.

II. Music has a remarkable power to shape our moods. A delicate, slow melody can bring relaxation or peace, while an energetic rhythm can awaken excitement or tension. Filmmakers skillfully use soundtracks to influence how viewers interpret a scene’s atmosphere. According to neuroscientists, musical sounds stimulate the brain to produce substances such as dopamine — a chemical closely linked to pleasure, motivation, and reward. In this way, music does not merely reflect emotions; it actively alters them by changing our brain activity.

III. In modern medicine, music has earned recognition as a tool for recovery and psychological well-being. Hospitals increasingly use music therapy to reduce anxiety, enhance sleep quality, and stabilize blood pressure. For patients coping with mental health conditions or memory disorders like Alzheimer’s disease, familiar tunes often evoke a sense of comfort and help them recall happy experiences. Through these effects, music supports both emotional healing and physical rehabilitation, proving itself to be a natural form of therapy.

IV. Technological development has completely transformed how people consume and share music. In earlier times, audiences relied on live performances or purchased physical recordings. Now, digital platforms and streaming apps allow instant access to millions of songs from anywhere in the world. This convenience has revolutionized listening habits, making music highly personalized and ever-present. However, it has also weakened the collective experience once found in communal listening — at concerts, festivals, or family gatherings. Technology has expanded availability but reduced the shared social aspect of music.

V. Music holds an extraordinary ability to awaken memories long forgotten. A single familiar tune can transport someone back to a wedding, a childhood celebration, or a distant holiday. Scientists explain that music stimulates both emotional and memory-related regions of the brain simultaneously, allowing old experiences to resurface vividly. This is why people with memory loss can often recall lyrics or melodies even when other recollections have faded. Music serves as a key to unlock emotional and autobiographical memories.

VI. Whether performed in a Tokyo concert hall, sung in a Peruvian village, or played by an orchestra in Vienna, music resonates across humanity. It surpasses linguistic boundaries and unites listeners from every corner of the world. At global celebrations such as the Olympic Games, songs inspire collective emotion and a sense of belonging among diverse audiences. Music reminds us of our shared human experience, acting as a bridge between cultures and nations.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

THE INVENTION OF THE CAMERA

Photography is so common today that people rarely stop to consider how revolutionary the invention of the camera truly was. From simple family snapshots to scientific discoveries, cameras have shaped how we see and record the world. Yet the history of photography stretches back far before the first photograph was taken.

The earliest concept of the camera came from a simple optical principle known as the camera obscura, meaning “dark chamber” in Latin. Ancient philosophers in China and Greece discovered that when light passes through a small hole into a dark room, it projects an upside-down image of the outside scene on the opposite wall. Artists in the Renaissance used this device to trace realistic images, but the pictures faded immediately.

That changed in the early 19th century. In 1826, a French inventor named Joseph Nicéphore Niépce managed to capture the first permanent image using a metal plate coated with a special chemical. However, his process required prolonged time of exposure to light. A few years later, Louis Daguerre, also French, refined the technique and introduced the daguerreotype, which produced clearer pictures in a fraction of the time. His invention quickly spread across Europe and the United States, marking the true beginning of photography as both an art and a science.

The next great leap came when photographic negatives were invented. British scientist Henry Fox Talbot developed a process called the calotype, which used paper coated with light-sensitive chemicals. Unlike Daguerre’s method, the calotype created a negative image that could be reproduced numerous times. This idea — making many prints from one negative — became the foundation of modern photography.

By the late 19th century, cameras were becoming smaller and easier to use. American entrepreneur George Eastman revolutionized photography by introducing roll film and launching his company, Kodak, in 1888. His slogan, “You press the button, we do the rest,” showed how simple photography had become. Now, anyone could capture moments of their lives without technical knowledge. This shift transformed photography from a scientific process into a popular hobby.

In the 21th century, cameras evolved rapidly. Portable film cameras were replaced by instant Polaroids, and later by digital devices that stored thousands of images on memory cards. Today, smartphone cameras combine sophisticated lenses and computer software to produce high-quality photos instantly. While the technology has changed dramatically, the goal remains the same: to preserve a moment in time.

The invention of the camera did more than create images — it changed human memory. People could now record their lives, share experiences, and even witness events they never attended. From documenting wars to capturing the first steps on the moon, cameras have not only reflected history but have also helped shape it.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE 'FLOW STATE'

In the landscape of human psychology and productivity, few concepts are as sought-after as the 'flow state'. Coined by psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, flow describes a state of complete immersion in an activity, where one feels energized, focused, and enjoys the process immensely. It is often referred to as being "in the zone." During flow, your sense of self seems to vanish, your perception of time becomes distorted—hours can feel like minutes—and your concentration is so absolute that all other distractions fade away. This ephemeral state is not just the peak of productivity; Csikszentmihalyi's research suggests it is also the peak of human happiness, a key component of a life well-lived.

Achieving this state, however, is not a matter of chance. It requires a specific set of conditions to be met. First, the activity must have clear, moment-to-moment goals. One must know what they are doing and why they are doing it, providing a clear path forward. Second, the activity must provide immediate and unambiguous feedback, allowing for continuous adjustments. A musician knows instantly if they've hit a wrong note; a rock climber knows if their grip is secure. This constant feedback loop keeps the person engaged and focused on the present.

Perhaps the most crucial condition is maintaining a delicate equilibrium between the challenge of a task and the skill of the individual. If the task is too easy relative to one's skills, it leads to boredom and apathy. Conversely, if the task is too hard, it leads to frustration. The flow state exists in the narrow channel where the task is just challenging enough to stretch your existing skills, forcing you to grow and adapt without becoming overwhelmed. It is this perfect balance that makes the experience so compelling and rewarding.

The neurological foundations of flow are equally fascinating. Brain imaging studies suggest that during a flow state, the brain experiences something called 'transient hypofrontality'. In simpler terms, the prefrontal cortex—the part of the brain responsible for our sense of self and our nagging inner critic—temporarily quiets down. This neurological shift explains the loss of self-consciousness and the silencing of self-doubt. Simultaneously, the brain is flooded with a cocktail of performance-enhancing and pleasure-inducing neurochemicals, including dopamine which sharpens focus and generates a feeling of deep satisfaction.

The implications of cultivating flow are profound. It is the antidote to the apathy often experienced during passive leisure, such as scrolling through social media or watching television. By actively seeking out activities that induce flow—be it in our work, hobbies, or even in deep conversation—we engage in tasks that are intrinsically motivating. This pursuit not only enhances our skills and productivity but also contributes significantly to our overall sense of well-being and fulfillment.

THE INFLUENCE OF SOCIAL MEDIA

I. Studies suggest that social media can have both positive and negative effects on mental health. While it allows people to stay connected, it can also lead to anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem, especially when users compare themselves to others. Additionally, excessive social media use has been linked to sleep disturbances and reduced productivity. Spending long hours online may also reduce time spent on physical activity, further impacting overall well-being.

II. One of the key explanations why people spend so much time on social media is because it is designed to be addictive. Features like endless scrolling, notifications, and personalized content trigger dopamine release in the brain, making it difficult to stop. These platforms use sophisticated algorithms to keep users engaged for as long as possible. This design can make it challenging for individuals to control their usage, leading to habitual checking throughout the day.

III. Many users rely on social media for news, but not everything they read is accurate. The spread of fake news has become a major issue, influencing public opinion and even political decisions. False information can be shared rapidly, making it challenging to distinguish between credible sources and misleading content. Users are encouraged to verify information with multiple trustworthy sources before forming opinions.

IV. Social media influencers have become incredibly powerful in marketing and public relations. With millions of followers, they can shape opinions on fashion, technology, and even political issues. Their endorsements often lead to significant trends, affecting consumer behavior and cultural movements. Influencers can also promote social causes and awareness campaigns, reaching audiences that traditional media may not.

V. While social media connects people across the world, it can also harm real-life relationships. Many people find themselves distracted by their phones during face-to-face conversations, leading to a decline in meaningful social interactions. Over time, this can weaken personal connections and create feelings of isolation. Excessive use may also reduce empathy and listening skills, making communication less effective.

VI. Short-form video content, such as TikTok and Instagram Reels, has become one of the most popular trends in social media. These quick, engaging videos appeal to short attention spans and are often designed to be highly shareable. As a result, brands and creators are increasingly focusing on producing concise, attention-grabbing videos to maximize audience engagement. The popularity of these videos has also influenced how information and entertainment are consumed, favoring shortness over depth. Critics warn that constant exposure to short-form content may reduce attention span over time.

DESERT TRAVELS

I checked my mobile phone and then looked towards the dirt path lit by our car lights. ‘It should be to our left,’ I said. We were passing through a small village, trying to reach the place I’d entered on my phone’s Global Positioning System (GPS).

Within minutes, we spotted what we were looking for. My companion stopped the vehicle. We looked into the night as our eyes got used to the dark and the view. We’d arrived at the start of our adventure. The plan was straightforward: leave the car and carry enough food and water in our backpacks to last a few days, and set out across the desert until we reached the road. And we’d chosen to do all this at the time of a full moon, which meant we could start our journey and walk mainly in the cool of the night. However, we wouldn’t set off on our desert adventure just yet. We put up the tent that we’d picked up while buying food at a local shop before setting off. The tent wouldn’t protect us from wind or rain, but it wasn’t complicated to put together, didn’t weigh much and cost less than a CD. Most importantly, it gave us somewhere to get a few hours’ rest.

We got up under the moonlight, lifted our backpacks and walked across some rough ground towards the sand. Our route was easy – we simply had to go east. We recorded how far we’d gone on my phone’s GPS, and checked our progress by counting the dunes – the great hills of sand that rose up like mountains across the desert. My GPS told me exactly how many there would be in total. Although it was still the early hours of the morning it was already hot, but we could just about handle it. After the night had passed, and as the sun moved higher in the sky, the heat became more unkind. There was no wind and no shade, but we carried on.

It is tiring to walk uphill; to do so with a heavy backpack is harder still, and walking on sand makes the whole experience almost impossible. I knew I had to save my energy, and even though I’d carefully planned what to take on the trip, at that point in time I was sure I’d got it wrong. I was glad, however, that I’d taken along two walking sticks.

These sticks actually served several purposes. As mid-morning approached, we stopped at the first tree we saw. We used it, my walking sticks and an old sheet to give us some shelter from the sun, resting as we waited for the cruel heat of the day to pass. It was only day one, and I already felt a strange mixture of excitement and exhaustion.

THE FUTURE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HEALTHCARE

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing the healthcare industry, offering groundbreaking solutions that were once thought impossible. From diagnosing complex diseases to enhancing treatment plans and managing patient data, AI is transforming medical practices worldwide. Advanced AI-powered algorithms can now process vast amounts of medical data within seconds, making disease detection not only faster but also more precise. Machine learning models, for example, have demonstrated exceptional accuracy in identifying cancerous tumors in radiology scans. In many cases, their diagnostic performance is comparable to, or even superior to, that of experienced medical professionals.

As AI continues to improve, its role in predictive analytics is becoming increasingly important, helping doctors detect illnesses in their early stages before they become critical. Despite these remarkable advancements, the integration of AI in healthcare is not without its challenges. One major concern is data privacy, as AI systems rely on extensive patient records to function effectively. Ensuring that sensitive medical information is securely stored and ethically used remains a top priority for both medical institutions and regulatory bodies.

The risk of data breaches and unauthorized access has raised serious ethical and legal concerns, prompting calls for stricter data safety policies. Additionally, algorithmic bias is another matter that must be addressed. If an AI system is trained primarily on data from a specific demographic, it may struggle to provide accurate results for individuals outside that group. This bias can lead to disparities in healthcare outcomes and reinforce existing inequalities in medical treatment.

Another pressing issue is decision-making autonomy in medical practice. While AI can offer valuable insights and recommendations, it lacks human judgment and the ability to consider the full complexity of a patient’s condition. Doctors still play a crucial role in interpreting AI-generated results and ensuring that medical conclusions align with a patient’s unique needs.

Ethical concerns also arise when AI is used in life-or-death situations, such as critical surgeries or emergency care. If an AI-driven diagnosis or treatment leads to a fatal mistake, determining accountability becomes a complex issue. Should the blame fall on the medical professional overseeing the AI, the developers who designed the system, or the hospital that implemented the technology? These questions remain at the forefront of AI ethics discussions.

Despite these challenges, AI continues to reshape the healthcare industry at an unprecedented pace. The development of deep learning and robotic surgery has opened new possibilities for patient care, making procedures less invasive and recovery times shorter.

Additionally, AI is being used to streamline hospital operations, optimize resource allocation, and even predict disease outbreaks before they occur. As research in this field advances, AI’s potential in medicine is expanding rapidly, promising a future where medical treatments are more precise, efficient, and accessible to people around the world.

YOUR DAILY DECISIONS

I. Ever walked into a store for one item and left with ten? That’s not an accident. Supermarkets are designed to make you spend more. Essentials like milk and bread are placed at the back, so you have to walk past tempting products first. Brightly colored displays, strategic lighting, and background music all influence how long you stay and how much you buy.

II. Have you ever noticed that some brands "feel" more trustworthy than others? That’s because companies use psychological tactics to create a sense of reliability. Simple logos, familiar colors, and friendly-sounding slogans all work together to make customers feel comfortable. Some brands even use specific scents in stores to trigger positive emotions.

III. People often assume they choose their favorite colors randomly, but science suggests otherwise. Studies show that certain colors are linked to emotions—blue can create feelings of calm, red increases excitement, and yellow grabs attention. That’s why fast-food chains use bright colors to make food seem more appealing, while luxury brands often stick to black and gold for sophistication.

IV. Why do we feel you have to buy something just because others are? The fear of being left out plays a huge role in decision-making. Whether it’s buying the latest gadget or trying a new trend, people tend to follow the crowd. Marketers take advantage of this by showing customer reviews, "best-seller" tags, and influencer endorsements to make products seem more desirable.

V. Streaming platforms use complex algorithms to keep you watching. Features like autoplay, personalized recommendations, and countdown timers between episodes trick your brain into staying longer. Every time you finish a show, the platform immediately suggests another, creating an endless loop of entertainment that’s hard to break.

VI. If a store tells you a sale is ending soon, do you feel the urge to buy something immediately? That’s because our brains react to scarcity. Limited-time deals, countdown timers, and "only a few left in stock" messages make people act fast. It’s a powerful marketing tool that creates urgency—even when there’s no real rush.

PART 4Questions 21–29

Read the following text for questions 21-29.

OUR SHOPPING HABITS

If you have ever been shopping and thought you were getting a bargain simply because the price appeared in red, or have left a shop because the sales assistant talked too much, you’re not alone. In fact, your actions are quite typical, according to experts on customer behaviour.

When it comes to shopping, experts explain that women think about everything much more carefully than men. A recent study showed that when men saw an advertisement with the prices written in red, they believed the shop was offering greater price savings than those printed in black. They felt very positive about buying the product as well.

In contrast, red didn’t have the same effect on female shoppers. It actually made them suspicious. Experts explain that if women see an ad in red, they question what’s happening and think they have to be extra careful. ‘Am I being tricked?’ they will ask themselves. Women also seem to have a much better memory than men when it comes to the prices in advertisements.

This could be because men don’t think so hard about adverts or because they just aren’t that interested.

In a separate study, it was found that customers seem to prefer sales people who can correctly read moods. This is news for managers who believe that sales will increase if shop assistants are always happy and friendly to customers. Researchers believe that the findings suggest that customers don’t always want sales staff to be extremely happy and chatty. Instead, we prefer staff who understand body language.

The key to a successful sale, then, is reading the customer’s mood and matching that mood. The experts explain that it isn’t advisable to match the mood of a customer who’s angry; a customer who is in a hurry or in a bad mood would rather deal with a sales person who understands them, can serve them quickly or just leave them alone – and not try to get them to chat about their family.

There are of course some factors which are outside the control of shop owners – like the weather, which can really change people’s moods. Experts are confident that good weather means good news for shop owners.

As much as 60–80% of customer decisions are made while people are actually in a shop, rather than before or after their visit. And as more people are out and about during nice weather, there is a higher chance they are shopping and therefore more opportunity for shops to make a sale. Rain and snow have the opposite effect, as people prefer to stay at home.

Another interesting finding from recent research is the growing impact of online shopping environments on customer psychology. Just like in physical stores, colours, layout, and tone of communication can influence buyers’ emotions and choices. For instance, websites that use bright colours and simple designs often make shoppers feel more confident about their purchases, while those that appear cluttered or confusing may cause hesitation. Moreover, customer reviews and ratings now play a major role in decision-making — far more than traditional advertising. This shows that, whether shopping online or in-store, people’s feelings and perceptions remain key drivers of their buying behaviour.

PART 5Questions 30–35

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

A SCIENTIFIC PIONEER

Marie Curie, born in 1867 in Warsaw, Poland, was a physicist and chemist whose groundbreaking work on radioactivity earned her two Nobel Prizes. From an early age, she demonstrated an exceptional aptitude for science, but as a woman in the late 19th century, she faced numerous barriers to higher education in her home country. Determined to pursue her passion, she moved to Paris to study at the Sorbonne, where she excelled despite financial hardships.

Curie’s research, conducted alongside her husband Pierre Curie, led to the discovery of two new elements, polonium and radium. Her work revolutionized the scientific understanding of radiation and its potential applications, particularly in medicine. However, prolonged exposure to radioactive materials took a toll on her health, leading to her death in 1934. Despite the risks, her discoveries paved the way for life-saving treatments such as radiotherapy, applied to combat cancer.

In addition to her scientific achievements, Curie played a crucial role in World War I by developing mobile X-ray units identified as "Little Curies," which were used to diagnose battlefield injuries. She trained medical personnel to operate these machines, ensuring that wounded soldiers received proper treatment. Her contributions to medical science extended beyond her own discoveries, as she influenced upcoming generations of scholars and physicians.

Marie Curie remains an inspirational figure in science, not only for her findings but also for breaking gender barriers. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and remains the only person to have won in two different scientific fields. Her legacy lives on through the institutions she founded, including the Curie Institute, which continues to be a leader in medical research today. Curie’s life demonstrates the power of perseverance and dedication, proving that scientific progress often comes with personal sacrifice.

Throughout her career, Curie remained committed to the advancement of science and the promotion of education. She strongly believed in sharing knowledge and collaborated with fellow scientists worldwide. Despite facing skepticism and discrimination, she remained focused on her work, letting her discoveries speak for themselves. Her relentless pursuit of knowledge and dedication to scientific inquiry continue to inspire scientists, particularly women, to break barriers and pursue their passions in STEM fields.

PART 2Mock Test 1

Hello everyone! I'm here to tell you about our brand new school library. We're very proud of it, and I hope you'll all make good use of it this year. First of all, let me introduce myself. I'm your new librarian, and my name is Sarah Smith. It's S-A-R-A-H Smith.

First, let me explain how it works. All students can use the library for free, but there's a small fee of £5 if you want to borrow books to take home. You only need to pay this once for the whole year.

Now, what kinds of books can you find here? Well, we have a wide range. Of course, there are study books to help with your school subjects — English, science, history and maths — but we also have a large collection of novels, from adventure stories to modern teenage fiction. And if you're interested in hobbies, you'll find books on cooking, photography, travel and even sport.

About borrowing, you can take up to 4 books at a time. Please remember, books must be returned within 3 weeks. If you need them longer, just ask, and we can usually extend the date. But if you don't bring them back, you'll have to pay a small fine.

Finally, a word about using the library space. It's open every school day from 8 in the morning until half past 5 in the afternoon. It's a quiet place to read, study or do homework, so please keep your voices low. Computers are also available, but you must book a time if you want to use them. So, welcome to the library! I'm sure you'll find it useful, whether you're preparing for exams or simply enjoying a good story.

PART 3Mock Test 1

Speaker 1. I moved to an apartment in New York where I didn't know anyone, but I started to make friends at work. One evening when I was really tired, there was incredibly loud music coming from the apartment downstairs, so I went and asked for it to be turned down. The next day, there was a note through the door from Mark saying he hoped he hadn't spoilt my evening. And that's the great thing about him — he always acknowledges if he's in the wrong. Anyway, we discovered we both love basketball, and we started practising together. We became firm friends and still see each other, although we have less time for basketball these days.

Speaker 2. When I was 13, my dad said his new boss had a daughter of my age who he was sure I would get on with. They'd just moved and she'd started a new school and didn't know anyone in the area. Of course, when we did get together, we didn't get along. I was quite reserved and Alessia was full of herself. Later, when we were grown up, we met again through friends, and this time we hit it off. Now I appreciate the fact that life's never dull when she's around, as there's always some project she's just getting started on and is excited about. It's true that opposites attract, but you don't always realise it when you're young.

Speaker 3. I sometimes wonder where I'd be without Johnny, who always seems to be around to cheer me up when there's a crisis. He doesn't say much, and he doesn't want to hear anyone's problems, but nothing ever seems to get him down, and that's a great bonus in a friend. He was always like that. Before going to university, I spent 3 months cleaning offices, and I had to be there by 5 in the morning. Johnny was always on the same bus as me, as he was working in a bakery. By the time I got to work, we'd shared a few jokes, and I was starting to feel human and ready to start my day.

Speaker 4. I've got myself into deep trouble sometimes because I do love to gossip. I can't stop myself. Most other people can't bear to keep things to themselves either, but Anna is different. If you do tell her something in confidence, you know it won't go any further. She lives very near me now, but she used to live in Thailand. A few years ago, I was travelling round Southeast Asia on buses, and my friend arranged for me to stay with Anna, who she'd met at university. As soon as I met her, I knew she'd be a lot of fun. She's quite a bit older than me, but it doesn't seem to matter.

PART 4Mock Test 1

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our new sports campus! I'm really pleased to see so many of you here today. Please have a look at the map in front of you while I explain. So, let's begin right at the entrance. As soon as you come through the main doors, the first place you'll notice, just on your left-hand side, is the reception area. This is where our staff will greet you. You can ask for information, sign up for membership or book spaces for particular activities.

Now, from there, if you walk straight along the main corridor towards the far end on the right-hand side, you will come to the bike riding area. This is an outdoor space surrounded by trees, and it's designed both for practice sessions and for people who simply want to cycle in a safe environment. Just below the bike area, you'll find the training pool. Please don't confuse this with the larger indoor swimming pool, which is located in the south. The training pool is much smaller and is used mainly for lessons, for children, and also for people who are just learning how to swim.

If we move across to the opposite side of the map, in the bottom left-hand corner, above the basketball hall, you will see the tennis courts. These are large, open-air courts. Now, directly below the basketball hall, you'll see the badminton court. This is an indoor court and can be booked for singles or doubles games. Unlike tennis, you don't need to bring your own rackets; we can provide them at reception.

Finally, before we finish, let me draw your attention to the medicine room, which is in the bottom right corner, beside the indoor pool. This room is very important because if you ever have an accident or feel unwell, this is where you should go. So, that's a quick overview of the main areas. Take a few minutes now to look at the map again and ask me any questions before we start the tour.

PART 5Mock Test 1

Extract One

A: Guess what? I was going out for the day yesterday when I heard the most horrible noise.

B: Oh, what was it?

A: A huge lorry turning round.

B: What, outside your house?

A: Yeah, and he wasn't exactly careful about it either.

B: What happened then?

A: There was a large crunching noise. I thought he'd driven over my car.

B: Did he wreck it completely?

A: Well, to my astonishment, when he pulled away, the car didn't have a mark on it.

B: What was the noise then?

A: He'd completely flattened the streetlight. There was glass everywhere.

B: You must have been furious.

A: Well, surprisingly, I wasn't. The look on the driver's face was priceless. He was horrified at what he'd done. I realised he was dreadfully embarrassed, poor man.

B: What happened next?

A: He leapt out of the lorry, knocked on the door and apologised.

B: And then?

A: He called the electricity company. They sent someone within an hour. Live electricity is dangerous.

B: So everything was all right in the end?

A: Well, it didn't make much difference to me, apart from not getting out when I planned. I was relieved that no one was hurt.

Extract Two

A: So, what about the orangutan in the news recently?

B: Oh yeah, Marla. She's rather clever. Last week, she climbed out of her enclosure clutching her baby son and headed for the cafeteria.

A: Did that cause a stir at the zoo?

B: Well, surprisingly, none of the visitors seemed overly concerned. Marla was so absorbed with what she was doing that she posed no real threat to anyone. But she did gather an admiring audience once she settled down with some bananas she'd taken. But then, the baby is seriously cute.

A: So Marla was returned to her enclosure?

B: Well, as soon as she saw the vet arrive to catch her, she knew what was going on and just calmly loped back of her own accord. I thought it was extremely astute.

A: Amazing.

B: Mm, really astute. When she sees her curators are distracted, she'll take the keys from their pockets. But unlike some of the other orangutans, she doesn't like playing with sign cards. We give them symbols for things like food. She seems to be streetwise, socially clever, but doesn't deal in abstracts.

A: Fascinating.

Extract Three

A: While I was in Cornwall last week, I saw a stonemason working on a statue. He was so intent on his work that he was oblivious to the fact that he was attracting a crowd of onlookers.

B: Really?

A: And then, when he finally stopped, everyone wanted to strike up a conversation with him.

B: Why was that? Were they interested in buying something?

A: Well, I'm sure most of them could have afforded to buy stylish art like this. They looked like city businesspeople down for the weekend. But actually they wanted to ask questions about the materials he used.

B: So they were interested in what he was actually doing?

A: Exactly. And then they asked him about his background, and finally one woman said, ‘It must be great earning your living by using your hands.’

B: But a stonemason probably doesn't earn a huge amount, unless he's really well known.

A: That's right, though the woman said, ‘I wish I could afford to do something like that.’

B: Well, isn't it often the case that people in high-paid business jobs who spend their lives at a computer would love to do something more creative?

A: You've got a point there.

PART 6Mock Test 1

Good morning. I'm so pleased to see so many of you here. I love my profession, and I want to pass on some information to all of you who might want to focus on dance. There are two distinct career areas with different entry routes which I'd like to mention. Anyone wishing to do classical dance as a career needs to have attended classes from early childhood, so that may not be very helpful to some of you. It's very rare to be able to progress otherwise. Contemporary dance can be learnt later in life, however, and a number of colleges offer degrees in modern dance.

Look carefully before you choose a degree course and make sure it suits you. Most tend to focus on the academic and technical aspects of dance rather than the skills required for performance, so it will be up to you to keep practising while you're studying and attending lectures. And you'll also find you need to be networking all the time and working hard at your contacts. The more workshops you go to, the more people you'll meet, and some of them will be useful later on. Nobody is going to find jobs for you, you know, so you have to be willing to go out there and promote yourself.

I was always taught at college that getting a job was rarely about just turning up for an audition and being picked. The people choosing between dancers will realise that you are willing to learn and take direction if you arrive with questions to ask, and actually that's what lots of dancers fail to do, as they're concentrating so hard on their technique and how they look.

All dancers love their work, but another thing you'll soon learn is that you won't be able to dance all the time, not because of overwork or exhaustion, but because there are so many dancers out there that unemployment is a factor in every dancer's life, and you have to develop other skills as well to make money. You can combine performing with teaching, whether you set up classes yourself or work for an employer. Some dance agencies and government bodies have openings in administration, and there are often opportunities because not many dancers think it's creative enough.

A dancer's career can be short, and in any event rarely lasts beyond the age of 40. Accept this, and it won't stress you. And do remember that any injury, especially to the feet, back and legs, can have an impact and may reduce the length of career even further, so it's really important to understand your body and always take care not to push yourself too hard. Dancing's a fantastic career, but it's not an easy one. You have to be prepared to travel to get the work that suits you, particularly if you specialise in one type of dance. That's the only way to make a success of things, because the jobs won't come to you. OK, I'll pause there for a minute so you—

I was really lucky last year to have the opportunity to visit South Africa. It was absolutely the holiday of a lifetime. I went with my husband. He has some relatives who emigrated there recently, an uncle and some cousins, so we spent a bit of time with them, which was good. Oddly enough, my grandfather was actually born in Johannesburg, but he'd left before he was 10 years old. Still, that's always made me feel I have a connection with the country, and I've always wanted to go there.

The main impetus for our visit, however, was that our son's mad on sport, and his school had organised a tour so the boys in the first and second teams could play some rugby matches there. Quite a few of us parents decided to go out there at the same time to watch them play, which was quite scary as the South African boys all seemed so much bigger than ours! But anyway, they all survived with no broken bones, and we managed to have a really exciting holiday too.

Although we were following the same route as the school tour, we travelled independently. The school used a travel agent called Rainbow Tours, and they were able to make arrangements for us too. We considered organising our trip through another company called Safari Holidays, but didn't use them in the end, though they also had some very good deals.

It was an amazing country. As soon as I got off the plane after our overnight flight, I was impressed by the light there. It was just so clear, quite different from what we have here. It was beautifully warm too, of course, but we'd been expecting that.

One of the best things we did was spend a weekend at a safari park. That was just brilliant. It was such a privilege to see so many beautiful animals in their natural habitat — black and white rhinos, giraffes, elephants, aardvark. I loved seeing lions sleeping in the bush. Best of all for me were the cheetahs, which we saw when we went on a night drive. My husband's favourites were the hippos.

We saw interesting animals elsewhere as well as at the safari park. We hired a car to get around, and we caught sight of lots of zebras and ostriches as we were driving along the east coast. One day we broke our journey at a crocodile farm and learnt so much about them.

PART 6Mock Test 3

When people talk about marketing, branding often comes up as one of the most influential factors. It’s not just about having a recognizable logo or catchy slogan—branding can actually shape how a company performs in its industry. A strong brand helps a business stand out and, in many cases, even take the lead in its particular market. Think of Apple. Their products are known not only for their design and functionality but also for the reputation they’ve built over time. Customers associate Apple with high quality, and that perception adds value. It’s why people are willing to pay more—they’re not just buying a phone or a laptop, they’re buying into an experience. And that experience is often emotional. Many brands don’t rely solely on logic or technical specifications to attract buyers. Instead, they tap into feelings. Coca-Cola is a good example. When someone drinks it, they’re not thinking about the ingredients. What they connect with is the feeling of happiness—a mood the brand has carefully cultivated through its advertising and global presence. In the online world, branding takes on a slightly different form. Digital businesses use tools to understand what their customers like. One common method is tracking browsing behavior through cookies. These small data files help companies learn about user preferences, which allows them to personalize recommendations and improve the overall shopping experience. And it’s not just about making things easier for the customer. This kind of insight can lead to better sales. When people feel that a brand understands them, they’re more likely to return, make purchases, and even recommend it to others. That’s the power of branding—it builds trust, creates emotional connections, and drives business forward. So, whether it’s through storytelling, smart data use, or a reputation for excellence, branding remains a central pillar of modern marketing.

Lecturer: During today’s seminar we will be looking at English Gothic architecture and its origins with a specific case study of Wells Cathedral in England. The Gothic style was initially brought over to England from France. This was at a period of time in which England was ruled from France by the Normans, starting with William the Conqueror who first defeated the English army at the Battle of Hastings on October 14th, 1066. After 1072 when some smaller rebellions in northern England had been defeated, the Normans gained complete control of the English monarchy, which they controlled until 1154. The peace that ensued in England had a large impact on many aspects of daily life. Thousands of French words entered the English language for the first time such as beef, fruit, city and hour. French ideas and styles, like Gothic, also began to flow across The Channel to England too, examples of which can still be seen in the architecture of many listed buildings. A listed building is one that is protected from alteration or demolition because of its historical or stylistic importance. One such building is Wells Cathedral. Construction on Wells Cathedral began in 1175 at a time when Gothic architecture as a style was in its infancy. As a result, it is one of the first entirely Gothic buildings ever constructed. From the first designs to the date, it was completed in 1490, Gothic architecture flourished in England. Therefore, later additions to the building were still influenced by this Gothic style, rather than by later architectural styles such as Tudor architecture. Older cathedrals in England would have initially been influenced by Romanesque architecture, alternatively known as Norman architecture in England. As the former name suggests, Romanesque was a building style based on the skills passed on to various areas of Europe by the Romans. When the Western Roman Empire collapsed in the 5th Century, these methods were retained by Rome’s former colonies and developed further. One such Roman gift to the Romanesque architects was the round arch, also known as the true arch. The Romans perfected this style by using wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs, which created pressure that held the structure together at the top. Cathedrals in England such as the ones in Ely and Canterbury were started before the arrival of Gothic

architecture. Even though parts of those two cathedrals which were constructed later are in the Gothic style, other sections predating the arrival of Gothic architecture are Romanesque. The result is known as eclectic because the building is constructed using more than one style. All of these cathedrals belong to a group known as the medieval cathedrals of England. There are twenty-six different buildings that belong to this group in total; all of which were constructed or added to during a five-hundred-year period from 1040 to 1540.

PART 6Mock Test 8

Mars has fascinated scientists and explorers for decades. But while the idea of sending humans there is exciting, the reality is far more complex. A round-trip mission could take many months, and just reaching the planet itself requires a significant amount of time—far longer than a single day. That kind of journey demands careful planning and resilience. One of the biggest concerns is the environment beyond Earth’s protective shield. Without the benefit of our atmosphere, astronauts are exposed to intense radiation, which can be harmful over long periods. Shielding and monitoring systems are essential to reduce the risks. Then there’s the financial side. Developing spacecraft, life support systems, and safety protocols for interplanetary travel comes at a steep price. It’s no surprise that missions like these are considered extremely expensive, often requiring international collaboration and years of investment. But it’s not just technical or financial challenges. The human aspect is equally important. Spending months in confined quarters, far from family and familiar surroundings, can lead to feelings of isolation. Maintaining mental health and team morale becomes a top priority. Of course, not everyone agrees that space exploration should be a priority. Some argue that the resources used for missions to Mars could be redirected to address urgent issues here on Earth—like poverty, education, or healthcare. It’s a debate that continues to shape public opinion and policy. And finally, there’s the question of safety when it comes to Martian soil. Scientists are cautious about the possibility of unknown microbes—tiny organisms that might exist on Mars and could pose risks if brought back to Earth. That’s why strict containment procedures are part of every sample-return plan. Despite these challenges, the dream of exploring Mars remains strong. Each step forward brings us closer to understanding our place in the universe—and what it might take to live on another world.

Lecturer: In the last lecture, we looked at the adverse effects of desert dust on global climate. Today we’re going to examine more closely what causes dust storms and what other effects they can have.

As you know, dust storms have always been a feature of desert climates, but what we want to focus on today is the extent to which human activity is causing them. And it is this trend that I want to look at, because it has wide-ranging implications. So – what are these human activities? Well, there are two main types that affect the wind erosion process, and thus the frequency of dust storms. There are activities that break up naturally wind- resistant surfaces such as off-road vehicle use and construction and there are those that remove protective vegetation cover from soils, for example, mainly farming and drainage. In many cases the two effects occur simultaneously which adds to the problem. Let’s look at some real examples and see what I’m talking about. Perhaps the best-known example of agricultural impact on desert dust is the creation of the USA’s ‘dust bowl’ in the 1930s. The dramatic rise in the number of dust storms during the latter part of that decade was the result of farmers mismanaging their land. In fact, choking dust storms became so commonplace that the decade became known as the ‘Dirty Thirties’. Researchers observed a similar, but more prolonged, increase in dustiness in West Africa between the 1960s and the 1980s when the frequency of the storms rose to 80 a year and the dust was so thick that visibility was reduced to 1,0 metres. This was a hazard to pilots and road users. In places like Arizona, the most dangerous dust clouds are those generated by dry thunderstorms. Here, this type of storm is so common that the problem inspired officials to develop an alert system to warn people of oncoming thunderstorms. When this dust is deposited it causes all sorts of problems for machine operators. It can penetrate the smallest nooks and crannies and play havoc with the way things operate because most of the dust is made up of quartz which is very hard. Another example – the concentration of dust originating from the Sahara has risen steadily since the mid-1960s. This increase in wind erosion has coincided with a prolonged drought, which has gripped the Sahara’s southern fringe. Drought is commonly associated with an increase in dust-raising activity but it’s actually caused by low rainfall which results in vegetation dying off.

I’m going to report on a case study of a programme which has been set up to help rural populations in Mozambique, a largely agricultural country in South-East Africa. The programme worked with three communities in Chicualacuala district, near the Limpopo River. This is a dry and arid region, with unpredictable rainfall. Because of this, people in the area were unable to support themselves through agriculture and instead they used the forest as a means of providing themselves with an income, mainly by selling charcoal. However, this was not a sustainable way of living in the long term, as they were rapidly using up this resource. To support agriculture in this dry region, the programme focused primarily on making use of existing water resources from the Limpopo River by setting up systems of irrigation, which would provide a dependable water supply for crops and animals. The programme worked closely with the district government in order to find the best way of implementing this. The region already had one farmers’ association, and it was decided to set up two more of these. These associations planned and carried out activities including water management, livestock breeding and agriculture, and it was notable that in general, women formed the majority of the workforce. It was decided that in order to keep the crops safe from animals, both wild and domestic, special areas should be fenced off where the crops could be grown. The community was responsible for creating these fences, but the programme provided the necessary wire for making them. Once the area had been fenced off, it could be cultivated. The land was dug, so that vegetables and

cereals appropriate to the climate could be grown, and the programme provided the necessary seeds for this. The programme also provided pumps so that water could be brought from the river in pipes to the fields. However, the labour was all provided by local people, and they also provided and put up the posts that supported the fences around the fields.

PART 6Mock Test 11

Last month I spent some time at a Cheetah Conservation Centre in Namibia in South West Africa. Anyone can go. You don't need to be an expert but they emphasise that you have to be flexible - there's such a wide range of tasks you might be involved in. And of course, you need to be tolerant of high temperatures and able to walk on rough terrain. I'd always dreamt of sleeping under the African stars but there were so many strange noises I didn't really enjoy it. We had all our meals outside and made a proper camp fire and barbecued food on it - I wasn't particularly good at any of that but learning to bake bread was fantastic and I took on that role. The fire made it taste so much better than an indoor oven. And of course, the work was so interesting. Cheetahs are a bit like sports cars - designed for speed - they're long and slim rather than muscular like a lion or tiger and, unlike other members of the cat family, their paws are extremely narrow with claws which grip the ground in a similar way to a car tyre. They look quite similar to leopards but I soon learnt to tell them apart.

So, what was I actually doing? Well, I helped to follow the movements of the cheetahs. The data was collected in a special collar, which had been perfected after years of research. Scientists wanted a way of attaching something very light and small to the animals which could be powered by solar batteries and now they've done it. I was following three female and two male cheetahs. The equipment was only activated when the animal moved and it recorded where each cheetah was, which direction it was headed, and how fast it was moving, with the data being sent up to 300 times a second via radio signals. I'd always thought that cheetahs are such good hunters because they run so fast but in fact, I discovered that what gives them a huge advantage is their ability to 'turn sideways. This is something they can do in a second or so when they spot some food and it's that rather than the way they move forwards, which makes them so agile. We wanted to check on when the cheetahs preferred to hunt, expecting it to be the cooler ends of the day. This indeed was the case but our research showed that more hunting took place at dawn than at twilight and that some hunting was even done at night. We also looked at where the cheetahs spend their time. They're mostly seen in open grassland, only occasionally venturing among shrubs and trees. But in fact, what the tracking equipment unexpectedly revealed was that they also headed into thick vegetation sometimes, leaving the open ground. It was so interesting to learn more about these beautiful creatures and how they live. I'm really hoping I can return to the centre again next year.

The cycle path follows the river southwards. After a bit, you'll see the Ashington China factory, which closed in 1962. It now offers guided tours to the public, which is worth a visit. Hello, I'm going to give you some insight into what's actually involved in my job as a basketball trainer. What I enjoy most is seeing an athlete perform at a high level, knowing that I helped them get there. There are numerous challenges of course but most of the time things go smoothly unless there's a breakdown in communication. Everything goes wrong then - from training programmes right down to players' concentration - if the coaches, management, players and medical staff aren't on the same track. I was lucky enough to study sports science at college like you, and most of what we did is still relevant but there've been massive developments in the psychology of sport in areas such as the motivation for athletes to succeed. What is constant though is the human body - I'm grateful for all the hours we spent in those classes as I use my depth of knowledge every day, much more than practical skills. A large part of my job is obviously assessing injuries and interestingly although back problems put players out of the sport for greater lengths of time, it's damage to ankles which dominates. Longer term, some players have problems with their knees and that can end their career altogether. We have to assess new trends in sports training to see if they're really going to benefit our players. A lot of companies knock on our door with the latest equipment and training programmes to improve players' strength but I find they're not worth the money and it's more effective to concentrate on injury prevention and general health. That's what has the most impact on results. The daily exercise schedule I use with the team hasn't changed much over the years. Strangely enough, it's the simplest exercises which aim to help players' balance that are the most beneficial to their game. Around those we also do lots of practice on technique of course and individual skills. After a big series of matches, I keep an eye on the players as it's easier for them to switch off and get into bad habits. They'll be exhausted and they need some time to sleep and rest. I make sure I suggest a nutrition programme to help them restore the energy they've lost.

Every sports trainer implements a team's fitness programme in a different way. But what I have learned is that in order to get the best out of the players I have to understand their personalities and which method is going to best suit each one. Once I have the right methods for each one, their fitness levels will improve much faster and they will develop the skills they need. Of all the things I've talked about - having a flexible approach, a constant awareness of what's going on in the team and specialised knowledge - we shouldn't ignore a sense of humour. Without that, none of the rest will work - it's a very challenging job and things go wrong all the time - so you won't get far without it. Thank you very much for listening …
